nama_domain: Higher Education Restructuring (state-directed culling and re-engineering of university degree programmes: 'discipline and major setting adjustment and optimisation' / 学科专业设置调整优化). The Chinese case: 12,200 undergraduate programme points revoked or suspended versus 10,200 newly created across the 14th Five-Year Plan (2021-2025), against a Ministry of Education target of adjusting roughly 20% of all national programme points. Generic business management, design, humanities and foreign-language programmes were cut; artificial intelligence, robotics, embodied intelligence, low-altitude technology and engineering, carbon neutrality science and engineering, integrated circuits and brain-computer science were created in their place.
kategori: Pendidikan (Higher Education Policy). Cross-cutting with Industrial Policy (majors are set to feed 16 designated strategic industries), Labour Market Policy (programme survival tied to graduate employment rates), and Demography (shrinking birth cohorts will eventually shrink the student base). This item is the 'supply-side' mirror of the AI/Automation and Youth Unemployment items in this research set: those describe the labour-demand shock, this describes the state's attempt to re-engineer labour supply through the university catalogue.
tahun_mulai_china: Layered start dates. (1) 2018-2019 — the quiet beginning: MOE began publishing annual programme registration/approval results in which revocations became conspicuous, and in March 2019 approved the first batch of 35 universities to run the standalone Artificial Intelligence undergraduate major (code 080717T). (2) 2022 — provincial exit mechanisms: Jiangxi and Fujian pioneered employment-rate-based warning systems (yellow card / red card) that suspend enrolment in low-placement programmes. (3) FEBRUARY 2023 — THE DECISIVE POLICY MOMENT: five ministries led by MOE issued the 'Reform Plan for Adjusting and Optimising Discipline and Major Setting in Ordinary Higher Education Institutions' (普通高等学校学科专业设置调整优化改革方案), setting the explicit target of optimising and adjusting roughly 20% of national discipline-major setting points by 2025. (4) 28 AUGUST 2025 — escalation: the Central Education Work Leading Group (a Party body above the ministry, signalling top-level political ownership) issued the 'Action Plan for Adjustment and Optimisation of Discipline and Major Setting in Higher Education (2025-2027)', extending the campaign for another three years with six named action lines. (5) 2026 — institutionalisation: the 2026 undergraduate catalogue created an entirely new 'Interdisciplinary' (交叉学科) degree category, the first structural change to the catalogue's top-level architecture in decades.
pemain_kunci_china: STATE / PARTY ACTORS (this is a state-led trend with no private prime mover): Central Education Work Leading Group (中央教育工作领导小组) — issuer of the 2025-2027 Action Plan, which places the campaign under direct Party supervision rather than ministerial administration; Ministry of Education, Department of Higher Education (教育部高等教育司) — owner of the annual programme registration/approval cycle and the undergraduate major catalogue; National Development and Reform Commission and MIIT — suppliers of the 16 priority industry list that majors must map onto; provincial education departments (Jiangxi, Fujian, Anhui, Sichuan, Heilongjiang, Zhejiang, Chongqing and 8 pilot provinces) — operators of the red/yellow card employment-rate exit mechanisms and of regional 'major cluster' matching; MOHRSS — supplier of graduate placement (毕业去向落实率) data that determines which programmes die. UNIVERSITIES AS VISIBLE MOVERS: Fudan University (president Jin Li, who cut the humanities share of undergraduate intake from 30-40% to 20% in 2025 — the single most-cited symbolic act of the campaign); Beihang / Beijing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics and Harbin Institute of Technology (first movers on Low-Altitude Technology and Engineering, and on Embodied Intelligence); Renmin University, Tianjin University (brain-computer science), Sichuan University (integrated circuits plus 6 other new majors); the 499-621 institutions that now run an AI undergraduate major. DATA / INTERMEDIARY ACTORS: MyCOS (麦可思) — the graduate-employment survey firm whose 'red card major' lists shape public perception; Zhaopin and BOSS Zhipin — recruitment platforms whose data is used to justify cuts; gaokao advisory media (高考直通车, 自主选拔在线, 中国教育在线) which transmit the signal to families and thereby drive application behaviour faster than the formal policy does.
apa_yang_terjadi_di_china:
China is running the largest deliberate re-engineering of a national university curriculum portfolio in modern history, and it is doing it top-down, on a quota, against an industrial-policy target list, using graduate employment rates as the kill switch.

(1) THE HEADLINE NUMBERS. Across the 14th Five-Year Plan (2021-2025), Chinese universities added roughly 10,200 undergraduate programme points (专业点 — one major at one institution) and revoked or suspended roughly 12,200. Net contraction of ~2,000 programme points, cumulative churn exceeding 30% of the national stock. The annual adjustment ratio crossed 10% for the first time in 2025 (10.1%). This exceeded the original 2023 target of adjusting 'roughly 20%' by 2025 — the campaign overshot its own quota by half again.

(2) THE MECHANISM IS A QUOTA PLUS A CATALOGUE PLUS A KILL SWITCH. The catalogue: MOE maintains a binding national list of permitted undergraduate majors. Nothing can be taught that is not on it, and getting onto it requires ministerial approval. The 2025 catalogue contained 845 majors; the 2026 catalogue contains 883 majors across 13 categories and 92 major classes, with 38 new majors added in one year. The quota: the February 2023 five-ministry reform plan instructed the system to adjust ~20% of programme points by 2025, converting what would elsewhere be a slow academic process into a measurable administrative KPI with a deadline. The kill switch: provinces run employment-based exit rules. Jiangxi issues a yellow card (with enrolment-quota deductions) to any programme whose graduate destination rate falls below 50%, and a red card forcing enrolment suspension if it stays below 50% for two consecutive years. Anhui and Jiangxi also apply a rule that programmes with employment rates below 60% for 2-3 consecutive years are revoked outright. Jiangxi alone added 312 programme points and stopped or revoked 335 over five years.

(3) WHAT DIED. The casualty list is remarkably consistent year after year. Over 2020-2024 the five most-revoked majors were Information Management and Information Systems (160 programme points revoked — first place four years running), Public Affairs/Public Utilities Management (138), Information and Computing Science (123), Marketing (104), and Product Design (93). Extending back to 2018-2022 adds Clothing and Apparel Design (70) and Educational Technology (51). In 2024 alone the top five revoked were Information Management and IS (38), Marketing (34), Information and Computing Science (27), Network Engineering (26) and Product Design (24). The pattern: generic, low-differentiation, easy-to-open, cheap-to-run programmes in management, applied design, and soft-IT — precisely the programmes that mass-expansion-era universities opened because they needed no laboratories.

(4) WHAT WAS BORN. The 2025 catalogue added 29 majors including Low-Altitude Technology and Engineering (低空技术与工程), Carbon Neutrality Science and Engineering (碳中和科学与工程), Integrated Circuit Science and Engineering, Artificial Intelligence Education, Area and Country Studies, Ocean Science and Technology, Intelligent Molecular Engineering, and Medical Device and Equipment Engineering. The 2026 catalogue went further and created a thirteenth top-level degree category — 'Interdisciplinary' (交叉学科) — populating it with 11 relocated majors plus 4 brand-new ones: Embodied Intelligence (具身智能), Brain-Computer Science and Technology (脑机科学与技术), Future Robotics (未来机器人) and Interdisciplinary Engineering (交叉工程). Nine universities were approved for embodied intelligence in the first batch; six for low-altitude technology and engineering in 2025 under an explicitly 'extraordinary/fast-track' (超常规) approval procedure that bypassed the normal multi-year approval cycle.

(5) THE PROGRAMME PORTFOLIO IS NOW EXPLICITLY AN INDUSTRIAL-POLICY INSTRUMENT. A 30 June 2025 MOE notice instructed universities to aim programme setting at 16 designated industry fields: integrated circuits, artificial intelligence, biomanufacturing, quantum technology, new energy, new materials, low-altitude economy, embodied intelligence, autonomous driving, international law and foreign-related legal affairs, international communication, international organisations, fintech, health and eldercare services, culture and tourism, and modern logistics. Since 2024, eight provinces (Heilongjiang, Zhejiang, Chongqing among them) run a pilot matching programme setting to regional industrial clusters, producing 247 designated 'characteristic advantage major clusters' aligned to 100-billion- and trillion-yuan regional industries. The degree catalogue and the industrial plan are now the same document read in two directions.

(6) ELITE INSTITUTIONS ARE MOVING FASTEST AND MOST SYMBOLICALLY. Fudan University's president Jin Li announced that undergraduate humanities and social science intake would fall from 30-40% to 20% of the class, under the slogan 'refine the humanities, sharpen the sciences, strengthen engineering, renew medicine, enliven the interdisciplinary' (文科做精、理科做尖、工科做强、医科做新、交叉做活). The 2025 intake of 3,820 delivered exactly that: humanities and social sciences 776 (20.3%), sciences 737 (19.3%), engineering 778 (20.4%), medicine 765 (20.0%), interdisciplinary 764 (20.0%). When China's most prestigious liberal-arts university caps the humanities at one fifth, every provincial university reads it as permission.

(7) THE 2025-2027 ACTION PLAN EXTENDS THE CAMPAIGN WITH SIX ACTION LINES: extraordinary/fast-track layout of urgently needed disciplines for strategic emerging and future industries; strengthening of basic disciplines inside excellence-building schemes; incubation of emerging and interdisciplinary fields including demonstration interdisciplinary centres; optimisation of existing programmes, with formal warnings and mandated remediation for programmes showing insufficient social demand, declining training quality, or inadequate conditions; modernisation of curricular content with AI-empowered teaching; and reform of training models via National Excellence Engineer Academies.

(8) THE PARALLEL VOCATIONAL TRACK. The same logic is applied below the university tier: 27 new vocational education majors were added in 2026 covering AI, the low-altitude economy and humanoid robotics (first intake 2027), following ~40 new vocational majors added in the previous cycle, with a target of vocational undergraduate places reaching at least 10% of vocational higher education enrolment by 2025 and 33 new undergraduate-level vocational colleges approved, roughly half upgraded from existing vocational schools. The stated driver is a projected shortage of ~30 million skilled manufacturing workers.

(9) THE FORCING CONTEXT IS A GRADUATE JOBS CRISIS. China will produce 12.7 million higher education graduates in the 2026 cohort, up 480,000 year on year, into a campus recruitment market of roughly 5.67 million posts against 15 million-plus job seekers. Urban youth unemployment has run around 16%. The restructuring is therefore not only industrial policy — it is a legitimacy response to visible graduate unemployment, and it lets the state attribute the mismatch to bad majors rather than to weak aggregate demand.

fase_tren_di_china: BOOMING and INSTITUTIONALISED, moving toward MATURE-WITH-EARLY-BACKLASH. Phase reading by dimension: (a) POLICY INTENSITY — peak and still rising: the campaign was escalated in August 2025 from a ministerial reform plan to a Central Education Work Leading Group action plan running to 2027, which means the political ceiling has been raised, not lowered. (b) EXECUTION — booming: the 2025 adjustment ratio crossed 10% for the first time, and the 2026 catalogue introduced a wholly new degree category, so the machinery is accelerating rather than settling. (c) CRITICAL DISCOURSE — early backlash is now visible and tolerated: Chinese academic and mainstream media openly debate whether the humanities will 'disappear', whether AI programmes are being opened by herd behaviour at institutions without faculty or laboratories, what happens to teachers whose programmes are cut, and whether employment-rate metrics are a legitimate way to judge basic disciplines. Notably the 2025-2027 Action Plan itself contains a counterweight action line on strengthening basic disciplines — an implicit acknowledgement that the cutting had overshot. (d) OUTCOME EVIDENCE — immature: the first cohorts from the new majors have not graduated, and the one early datapoint available (55% field-relevant employment for 2024 AI graduates) suggests the new programmes may reproduce the mismatch they were built to solve. Expect the phase to shift to 'regulated/consolidating' around 2027-2028 when the Action Plan expires and the quality problems in the newly opened programmes become measurable.
puncak_tren_china: Two distinct peaks. POLICY PEAK: 28 August 2025, when the Central Education Work Leading Group — not merely MOE — issued the 2025-2027 Action Plan, elevating programme restructuring from education administration to Party-level strategic policy. VOLUME PEAK: 2025, the first year in which the annual adjustment ratio exceeded 10% of all programme points, closing a five-year period with >30% cumulative churn. SYMBOLIC PEAK: March 2025, Fudan University's announcement capping humanities and social science undergraduate intake at 20%, which functioned as the permission signal for the rest of the system and generated the largest public debate. CATALOGUE-ARCHITECTURE PEAK: 28 April 2026, creation of the 'Interdisciplinary' degree category with Embodied Intelligence, Brain-Computer Science and Technology and Future Robotics — the point at which the catalogue stopped being amended and started being rebuilt. GEOGRAPHIC CONCENTRATION: the cutting is heaviest in second- and third-tier provincial and private undergraduate institutions (Jiangxi, Anhui, Fujian, Henan, Shandong) that expanded fastest during the 1999-2015 massification and have the weakest programmes; the creation of new majors is concentrated in Beijing, Shanghai, Jiangsu, Guangdong, Zhejiang and Hubei where the target industries and the qualified faculty actually exist. The campaign therefore simultaneously downgrades the periphery and upgrades the core.
status_di_indonesia: BARU MULAI / EARLY AND VOLUNTARY, NOT A DIRECTED CAMPAIGN. Indonesia in mid-2026 has (a) the diagnosis, (b) ministerial rhetoric, (c) a small volume of bottom-up closures, and (d) the first strategic new programmes — but no quota, no national target, no employment-rate kill switch, and an explicit ministerial denial that programme closure is government policy. 122 study programmes were closed during 2026, all on the proposal of the host institutions themselves (both public and private), mostly because enrolment collapsed or the institution wanted to swap the programme for a more attractive one. Minister of Higher Education, Science and Technology Brian Yuliarto has publicly reframed the issue as 'transformation, not closure' — for example electrical engineering evolving into AI, machine learning or robotics tracks, with evaluation every 3-4 years — and has stated that closure is a last resort only where a programme fails quality standards and cannot be rescued through mentoring or transformation. Simultaneously the ministry defends basic sciences, social sciences, humanities and education programmes as holding an 'important position in the national talent architecture', explicitly rejecting the view of higher education as a narrow labour supplier. So Indonesia has arrived at the same problem statement as China circa 2019-2022 but has chosen, so far, the opposite instrument: persuasion, performance contracts and curriculum reform ('Diktisaintek Berdampak' / 'Kampus Berdampak', performance contracts signed for 2026) rather than catalogue control and forced exit. On the creation side Indonesia is genuinely moving: Universitas Indonesia's Academic Senate approved a standalone S1 Artificial Intelligence programme on 3 October 2025 for the 2026/2027 intake, UNIKOM opened S1 Robotics Engineering and AI for 2025/2026, and roughly 16 institutions now offer robotics-related programmes.
contoh_konkret_indonesia:
POLICY AND ACTORS: Kementerian Pendidikan Tinggi, Sains dan Teknologi (Kemdiktisaintek) under Minister Brian Yuliarto and Deputy Minister Fauzan; Secretary-General Badri Munir Sukoco, who put the teacher-education oversupply figures into public circulation at the National Population Symposium in April 2026; Director of Institutional Affairs Mukhamad Najib, source of the programme-count-by-field data (6 May 2026). Programme frameworks: 'Diktisaintek Berdampak' and 'Kampus Berdampak' (the successor framing to Kampus Merdeka), with 2026 performance contracts signed by hundreds of institutional leaders; new IKU (key performance indicators) for impact rather than graduate counts; vocational 'link and match with DUDIKA' curriculum grants for 2026.

CLOSURES (the Indonesian equivalent of China's 撤销): 122 programmes closed during 2026 on institutional proposal, discussed in parliament on 2 June 2026. The eight most frequently closed: D3 Midwifery (16 institutions), D3 Informatics Management (8), D3 Accounting (7), D3 Computer Engineering (3), D3 Nursing (3), D3 Finance and Banking (3), S1 Retail Management (3), S1 Mathematics (2). Note the pattern: overwhelmingly D3 diploma programmes being displaced by D4/S1, not a strategic cull. Separately, 84 private higher education institutions have been flagged for possible licence revocation for having unclear management, students or lecturers, and 23-25 private institutions have already had operating licences revoked for diploma fraud and phantom enrolment — this is Indonesia's real 'exit mechanism' and it is an integrity enforcement mechanism, not an industrial-policy one.

THE OVERSUPPLY CASE THAT COULD TRIGGER AN INDONESIAN VERSION: teacher education. Indonesia runs 6,844 education (kependidikan/keguruan) study programmes — the largest single field, ahead of engineering at 6,127 — producing roughly 490,000 graduates a year against roughly 20,000 teacher and early-childhood facilitator vacancies. Critics have described the ~6,000 education and religious studies programmes as a Ponzi structure that sustains itself by recruiting new students to pay for the last cohort. This is Indonesia's exact analogue of China's Information Management and Public Affairs Management problem, at larger scale.

NEW PROGRAMMES (the Indonesian equivalent of China's 新增): Universitas Indonesia S1 Kecerdasan Artifisial at Fasilkom, approved 3 October 2025, first intake 2026/2027, aligned to the National AI Strategy 2020-2045, taking Fasilkom to three undergraduate programmes (Computer Science, Information Systems, AI); UNIKOM S1 Teknik Robotika dan Kecerdasan Buatan from 2025/2026; roughly 16 institutions offering robotics-linked programmes; a national semiconductor talent programme coordinated through Kemenko Perekonomian and Kemdiktisaintek, including an Indonesia Semiconductor Hackathon 2026 and pushes for chip-design curricula and microelectronics laboratories; ITB's rare programmes such as Bioenergy and Chemurgy Engineering. At school level, Kurikulum Merdeka 2026 adds coding and artificial intelligence as elective subjects nationally — the pipeline precondition.

SYSTEM CONSTRAINTS THAT SHAPE ALL OF THIS: roughly 4,000+ higher education institutions, the great majority private; only about 6% of institutions hold 'Unggul' (excellent) accreditation as of end-2025; gross higher education participation rate around 32%.

estimasi_lag_tahun:
6-9 YEARS on policy formation; 10-15 YEARS on execution capability; and on one dimension the lag is effectively infinite because the instrument itself may never transfer.

DECOMPOSED:
(a) PROBLEM RECOGNITION — lag ~4-5 years. China's public debate about useless majors and graduate mismatch peaked around 2021-2022; Indonesia's equivalent debate (122 prodi, teacher-education oversupply, 'prodi tidak relevan') is a 2025-2026 phenomenon.
(b) FORMAL POLICY WITH A NUMERIC TARGET — lag ~6-8 years and counting. China set the 20%-by-2025 quota in February 2023. Indonesia as of mid-2026 has explicitly denied that programme closure is a policy. If Indonesia adopts a target-based approach it will most plausibly land around 2029-2031, giving a 6-8 year lag; if it never adopts one, this dimension does not converge.
(c) EXIT MECHANISM TIED TO GRADUATE OUTCOMES — lag ~7-10 years. Chinese provinces have run employment-rate red/yellow cards since 2022. Indonesia has accreditation (BAN-PT/LAM) and tracer studies but does not use graduate placement as a binding enrolment kill switch; the accreditation system already struggles, with only ~6% of institutions rated Unggul.
(d) OPENING STRATEGIC NEW MAJORS — lag ~7 years and NARROWING FAST. China approved the first 35 standalone AI undergraduate programmes in March 2019; Universitas Indonesia approved its S1 AI programme in October 2025 for a 2026 intake. That is a clean 6.5-7 year lag. For robotics the lag is similar (UNIKOM 2025). For newer categories — embodied intelligence (China 2026), low-altitude technology and engineering (China 2025), carbon neutrality science and engineering (China 2025) — Indonesia has no equivalent programme at all, so the lag on the current frontier is at least 5-8 years forward from now.
(e) EXECUTION CAPACITY — lag 10-15 years. Even where Indonesia opens the right programme names, the faculty, laboratories and industry partners that make them real are 10-15 years behind; China itself is discovering that 621 AI programmes do not equal 621 competent AI programmes, and Indonesia's version of that problem will be more severe because its private-institution tail is longer and thinner.

CONFIDENCE NOTE: this is one of the few items in this research set where the lag on the CREATION side (7 years) is much shorter than the lag on the DESTRUCTION side (indefinite). Indonesian universities can and do open AI majors quickly because opening a programme is a revenue opportunity; closing one destroys a yayasan's cash flow. Asymmetric incentives mean Indonesia will import half the Chinese model.
bukti_historical_lag:
(1) THE AI MAJOR ITSELF — the cleanest single measurement in this entire research set. China: MOE approved the first 35 universities to run the standalone Artificial Intelligence undergraduate major in March 2019; by 2024 the count was 621 institutions, making it the most-added major of the decade. Indonesia: Universitas Indonesia's Academic Senate approved a standalone S1 Kecerdasan Artifisial on 3 October 2025 for first intake 2026/2027 — and this is the flagship national university, i.e. the earliest possible adopter. Lag: 6.5-7 years, measured first-mover to first-mover.

(2) DATA SCIENCE / BIG DATA MAJORS. China added 数据科学与大数据技术 to the catalogue in 2016 and it spread to hundreds of institutions within four years. Indonesian universities (Telkom University, ITS, IPB, Binus and others) opened Sains Data / Data Science programmes from roughly 2020-2021. Lag: 4-5 years. This shorter lag is instructive — it shows the creation lag has been compressing across successive technology waves, from ~5 years (data science) to ~7 years (AI, distorted by pandemic-era approval delays).

(3) MASSIFICATION AND THE OVERSUPPLY IT PRODUCES. China's higher education expansion began with the 1999 enrolment surge; the resulting oversupply of cheap-to-run management and soft-IT programmes became a visible policy problem around 2018-2022, i.e. roughly 20 years later. Indonesia's private higher education expansion accelerated through the 2000s-2010s; its oversupply crisis (teacher education, D3 programmes, phantom campuses) became a visible policy problem in 2024-2026, roughly 20 years later on its own clock. The structural rhythm is identical, offset by the difference in when massification started — which is where much of the 6-9 year headline lag actually comes from.

(4) VOCATIONAL EDUCATION REFORM. China revised its Vocational Education Law in 2022 to give vocational education legal parity with general education and approved 33 new undergraduate-level vocational colleges. Indonesia's vocational reform (Kampus Vokasi, D4 conversion, link-and-match with DUDIKA) has been running since 2019-2020 in policy but the 2026 closure list shows the D3-to-D4 conversion is still in progress — Indonesia is arguably NOT behind here, and on vocational-general parity may be roughly simultaneous. This is the one sub-dimension where the lag is near zero.

(5) THE COUNTER-EVIDENCE — an area where Indonesia is genuinely earlier. Indonesia introduced Kampus Merdeka/MBKM in 2020, a large-scale curriculum-flexibility reform allowing students to take up to three semesters outside their programme. China has nothing structurally equivalent at national scale; its reform runs through the catalogue rather than through student choice. So the lag is not uniform: Indonesia is behind on state-directed portfolio control and ahead on student-level curricular flexibility. Any lag estimate that ignores this will overstate Indonesian backwardness.

(6) SIGNAL-TRANSMISSION EVIDENCE. Indonesian mainstream coverage of the Chinese 12,200-programme cull appeared within days of the June 2026 international reporting, and Indonesian education commentators immediately used it in the domestic 'tutup prodi' debate. The idea now travels in near real time even though the institutional capacity to act on it does not — a recurring pattern across this research set.
tipe_lag: LAGGARD (dominant), with a SELECTIVE-ADOPTION overlay and one REVERSE sub-dimension. Indonesia is a clear laggard on the state-directed, quota-driven, industrial-policy-aligned restructuring of the programme portfolio (6-9 years behind on policy, 10-15 on capability). It is a shorter-lag follower on opening new strategic majors (~7 years and compressing). It is roughly SIMULTANEOUS on vocational-education reform and on the general diagnosis of graduate mismatch. And it is REVERSE — ahead of China — on student-level curricular flexibility (MBKM/Kampus Merdeka, 2020) and on the political acceptability of defending humanities and basic sciences, which Indonesia's ministry states explicitly and China's ministry only implies through a counterweight action line. The most likely end state is not convergence but SELECTIVE ADOPTION: Indonesia imports the growth half of the Chinese model (open AI, robotics, semiconductor, green-energy programmes) and does not import the destruction half (forced closure of 20% of programmes), because the growth half is revenue-positive for institutions and the destruction half is existential for them. This produces a distinctive Indonesian failure mode — portfolio inflation rather than portfolio rotation — which is analysed under unintended_consequences.
probabilitas_transfer: SEDANG-TINGGI overall, but split sharply by component. Opening new strategic majors (AI, robotics, semiconductors, renewable energy, data science): TINGGI, ~90%, already happening. Rhetorical adoption of 'relevance to industry' as the governing criterion for programme evaluation: TINGGI, ~85%, already stated ministerial position. Systematic closure of low-demand programmes at meaningful scale: SEDANG, ~50% within a decade. A binding national numeric target on the Chinese model (e.g. 'restructure 20% of prodi'): RENDAH-SEDANG, ~30%. An employment-rate-based automatic exit mechanism with enrolment suspension: RENDAH, ~20-25%. Creation of frontier categories with no Indonesian industrial base (low-altitude engineering, embodied intelligence, carbon neutrality engineering, brain-computer science) as named degree programmes: RENDAH-SEDANG in the near term, ~35% by 2030, and likely to appear first as concentrations inside existing engineering degrees rather than as standalone programmes.
alasan_probabilitas:
WHY THE GROWTH HALF TRANSFERS EASILY (high probability): opening a programme in Indonesia is a revenue event for the institution and a prestige event for the rector, requires ministerial permit but no closure of anything, and is strongly pulled by student demand — Indonesian applicants track the same global signals about AI that Chinese applicants do, and rankings, accreditation KPIs and the 'Kampus Berdampak' performance contracts all reward visible modernity. Indonesia also has a genuine articulated national demand: the National AI Strategy 2020-2045, the semiconductor talent programme with Kemenko Perekonomian, the nickel/EV battery downstreaming agenda, and the renewable-energy transition all create at least a policy-level justification for new engineering programmes. The pipeline precondition is being laid at school level with coding and AI electives in Kurikulum Merdeka 2026.

WHY THE DESTRUCTION HALF TRANSFERS BADLY (low-to-medium probability): (1) OWNERSHIP STRUCTURE. The overwhelming majority of Indonesian institutions are private foundations (yayasan). A study programme is their product line and cash flow; closing it is not an administrative decision but a business death. China's cull worked because MOE controls enrolment quotas even at private institutions and because most of the affected capacity sat inside public provincial universities that the state funds directly. Indonesia's ministry has no equivalent lever over a yayasan's economics. (2) POLITICAL ECONOMY OF TEACHER EDUCATION. The single largest oversupply — 6,844 education programmes, ~490,000 graduates against ~20,000 vacancies — is also the most politically protected, entangled with LPTK institutional interests, PPG certification, honorary-teacher constituencies, professional associations and regional politics. Any move against it triggers immediate resistance, and the counter-narrative (Indonesia is short 679,000 teachers) is officially available from another ministry. (3) ACCESS EQUITY. With a gross participation rate of only ~32%, Indonesia's small regional private campuses are frequently the only tertiary access point in their kabupaten. Closing programmes there subtracts access in a country still trying to expand it, whereas China closed programmes in a system with a much higher participation rate and a shrinking birth cohort — China could afford contraction, Indonesia demographically cannot yet. (4) NO INDUSTRIAL DEMAND TO ROTATE INTO. China's cull was credible because the receiving industries — semiconductors, EVs, robotics, low-altitude aviation, renewables — actually exist at scale and hire. Indonesia lacks a domestic industrial base capable of absorbing large cohorts of AI, robotics or chip-design graduates, so a forced rotation would move students from a low-employment programme into a different low-employment programme. (5) STATE CAPACITY AND DATA. China's mechanism runs on annual, comparable, provincially audited graduate-destination data. Indonesia's tracer study coverage is uneven and self-reported; an employment-rate kill switch would be gamed within one cycle. (6) EXPLICIT MINISTERIAL POSITION. Kemdiktisaintek has stated that basic sciences, social sciences, humanities and education hold an important place in the national talent architecture and that higher education is not merely a labour supplier — the opposite of the framing that made China's cull possible.

NET: expect a high-volume, low-intensity Indonesian version — many new programmes, a slow trickle of voluntary closures concentrated in D3 programmes and in institutions that are already failing, and enforcement energy directed at integrity violations (phantom campuses, diploma fraud) rather than at strategic misalignment.
vektor_transmisi:
This trend transfers primarily as POLICY IDEA and INSTITUTIONAL MIMICRY rather than as capital or product, which makes its transmission vectors different from the commercial items in this research set.

(a) POLICY DIFFUSION AND OFFICIAL LEARNING — the primary vector. Indonesian ministries and university leadership consume Chinese education policy through bilateral education cooperation, Ministry of Education comparative studies, delegations to Chinese universities, and multilateral framings (World Bank, OECD, ASEAN education ministers' meetings) that increasingly cite China's programme restructuring as a reference case. The June 2026 international reporting on the 12,200-programme cull was picked up in Indonesian media within days and immediately entered the domestic 'tutup prodi' debate. Expect the Chinese model to be cited explicitly in Indonesian policy documents and DPR hearings within 1-2 years.

(b) ALUMNI, SCHOLARSHIPS AND ACADEMIC DIASPORA — a strong and underrated vector. Indonesia sends a large and growing number of students to China on CSC scholarships, Belt and Road education programmes, and university partnerships (Tsinghua, Zhejiang, Harbin Institute of Technology, Southeast University and provincial universities). These returnees enter Indonesian faculties and ministries carrying the Chinese curricular template — including the assumption that a degree programme should map to a named industry. Chinese-language and China-studies programmes in Indonesia, plus Confucius Institute successors, provide additional channel capacity.

(c) CHINESE INDUSTRIAL PRESENCE CREATING DERIVED CURRICULAR DEMAND — the most concrete vector. Chinese firms operating in Indonesia (Wuling, BYD, CATL and the Morowali/Weda Bay nickel-battery complexes, Huawei, Xiaomi, TikTok/ByteDance, Mixue's supply chain, Chinese EPC contractors on rail and power projects) create direct employer demand for specific skills and frequently fund or co-design vocational and university programmes to secure their own labour supply. Huawei's ICT Academy programme with Indonesian universities and polytechnics is the template; nickel-industry technical academies in Sulawesi are the heavy-industry version. This vector delivers curriculum change without requiring any Indonesian policy decision at all, and it is the single most likely route by which battery/metallurgy/automation programmes appear in eastern Indonesia.

(d) EQUIPMENT, PLATFORM AND CERTIFICATION EMBEDDING. Chinese hardware and software vendors seed laboratories and certification tracks — robotics kits, industrial automation trainers, cloud and AI platform certifications — which then define what a programme can actually teach. Whoever supplies the teaching laboratory writes the curriculum in practice. Chinese vendors compete here with US platform incumbents, and in vocational and second-tier institutions where price dominates, Chinese equipment increasingly wins.

(e) GLOBAL RANKINGS AND ACCREDITATION ISOMORPHISM — an indirect but powerful vector. As Chinese universities climb QS/THE rankings on the back of engineering and computer science output, Indonesian institutions chasing rankings replicate the same portfolio logic: expand engineering and computing, protect research-productive units, deprioritise low-output humanities. This produces Chinese-style outcomes through a non-Chinese mechanism.

(f) STUDENT AND PARENT DEMAND VIA ALGORITHMIC CONTENT — the fastest-moving vector. Indonesian applicants and parents encounter 'jurusan masa depan' and 'jurusan yang akan hilang' content on TikTok, YouTube and Instagram, much of it derivative of Chinese gaokao advisory content. Application patterns shift years before ministries act, and enrolment collapse is precisely the trigger that produced Indonesia's 122 voluntary closures in 2026. Demand-side transmission is therefore running ahead of policy-side transmission — the reverse of the Chinese sequence.

(g) WHAT IS NOT A VECTOR: Chinese venture capital and direct market entry, which drive most other items in this set, are largely irrelevant here. Higher education programme approval is a sovereign function, and foreign providers face tight restrictions in Indonesia. This is why the trend will arrive as an idea, slowly, rather than as a company, quickly.
prasyarat_struktural:
WHAT HAD TO BE TRUE IN CHINA FOR THE CULL TO HAPPEN, AND WHERE INDONESIA STANDS ON EACH:

(1) STATE CONTROL OVER ENROLMENT QUOTAS AND A BINDING NATIONAL MAJOR CATALOGUE. China: absolute — 883 permitted majors, ministerial approval for every programme point, provincial power to deduct enrolment quotas. Indonesia: partial — programmes require permits and accreditation, but there is no closed national catalogue and no routine quota instrument over private institutions. THRESHOLD NOT MET, and unlikely to be met without new legislation.

(2) A PUBLIC-DOMINANT INSTITUTIONAL BASE. China: the great majority of the affected capacity sits in public provincial universities, which the state funds and can therefore restructure. Indonesia: private institutions dominate by count and carry a very large share of enrolment. THRESHOLD NOT MET — this is the single most important structural difference.

(3) DEMOGRAPHIC HEADROOM TO CONTRACT. China's 18-year-old cohort is shrinking and its gross tertiary enrolment ratio is roughly 60%, so cutting capacity is compatible with continued access. Indonesia's gross participation rate is about 32% and its 18-24 cohort is still large; contraction here subtracts access rather than trimming excess. THRESHOLD NOT MET — Indonesia is at the stage of expansion China was in around 2005-2010, not the stage of consolidation China is in now. This alone justifies a substantial part of the estimated lag and argues that a full Chinese-style cull may never be appropriate.

(4) A RECEIVING INDUSTRIAL BASE. China: semiconductors, EVs, batteries, robotics, commercial drones/eVTOL, solar and wind manufacturing, all at world scale, hiring hundreds of thousands of engineers a year — which is what makes 'close marketing, open integrated circuits' a coherent instruction. Indonesia: nickel and battery midstream, EV assembly, a nascent chip-design ambition, digital platforms — real but 1-2 orders of magnitude smaller, and heavily weighted toward extraction and assembly rather than design. THRESHOLD PARTIALLY MET, and only in specific corridors (Morowali/Weda Bay, Karawang-Cikarang, Batam, Greater Jakarta).

(5) GDP PER CAPITA AND R&D INTENSITY. China's restructuring campaign began in earnest around 2023 at roughly USD 12,600 GDP per capita with R&D at ~2.6% of GDP. Indonesia in 2025-2026 sits at roughly USD 5,000-5,200 GDP per capita with R&D around 0.3% of GDP. On income Indonesia is roughly where China was in 2010-2011; on research intensity the gap is far wider and is the binding constraint, because a low-R&D economy has no employer capable of absorbing the graduates that a Chinese-style rotation would produce. THRESHOLD NOT MET on R&D.

(6) FACULTY SUPPLY IN THE TARGET FIELDS. China opened 621 AI programmes and is openly criticised for doing so with retrained faculty teaching from outdated materials. Indonesia has a far thinner pool of PhD-qualified faculty in AI, robotics, power electronics, semiconductor design and climate engineering, concentrated in perhaps 10-15 institutions. THRESHOLD NOT MET nationally; met only at ITB, UI, UGM, ITS, Telkom University, IPB and a handful of others.

(7) COMPARABLE, AUDITED GRADUATE-OUTCOME DATA. China: annual graduate destination rates by programme point, provincially audited, used to trigger red/yellow cards. Indonesia: tracer studies exist and feed accreditation but are uneven, self-reported and not used as a binding trigger. THRESHOLD NOT MET — and this is the most fixable item on the list, which makes it the highest-leverage policy target.

(8) POLITICAL PERMISSION TO DEVALUE THE HUMANITIES. China: available, and demonstrated by Fudan capping humanities intake at 20% without regime-level controversy. Indonesia: not available — the ministry has publicly defended humanities, social sciences, basic sciences and education as central to the national talent architecture, and Indonesian civil society, religious organisations and the pesantren/Islamic higher education sector would resist a technocratic devaluation of the humanities far more effectively than Chinese academics could. THRESHOLD NOT MET, arguably permanently, and this should be read as a feature rather than a deficiency.

WATCH-THRESHOLDS THAT WOULD SIGNAL THE TREND IS ARRIVING: gross participation rate rising above ~40% (removing the access objection); R&D intensity above ~0.6% of GDP; tracer-study data becoming mandatory, standardised and published per programme; and the first ministerial regulation that ties enrolment permission to graduate placement.

hambatan_transfer:
(1) OWNERSHIP AND FINANCE. Private foundations own most Indonesian capacity and depend on tuition per programme; closure is a solvency event, not an administrative one. There is no Indonesian equivalent of the state subsidy that let Chinese provincial universities absorb the shock of losing a programme.

(2) NO BINDING LEVER. Indonesia's ministry controls permits and accreditation but not enrolment quotas at private institutions. Accreditation was already weak leverage — only ~6% of institutions hold 'Unggul' status and the system tolerates the rest. Adding a new mandate to a regulator that cannot enforce existing standards is unlikely to work.

(3) ACCESS EQUITY AND GEOGRAPHY. At ~32% gross participation, closing regional programmes removes the only tertiary option in many districts, in an archipelagic country where students cannot easily relocate. China cut capacity from a position of abundance; Indonesia would be cutting from a position of scarcity.

(4) POLITICAL PROTECTION OF THE LARGEST OVERSUPPLY. Teacher education (6,844 programmes) is defended by LPTK institutional interests, teacher organisations, regional political interests, and by a competing official narrative that Indonesia is short 679,000 teachers.

(5) MISSING RECEIVING INDUSTRY. Rotating students into AI, robotics or semiconductors only helps if employers exist. With R&D at ~0.3% of GDP and an economy weighted toward commodities, construction and consumption, Indonesia risks rotating graduates from one unemployment queue into a better-branded one.

(6) FACULTY SCARCITY. Opening the new programmes requires PhD-qualified staff in fields where Indonesia has few. China is already criticised for staffing 621 AI programmes with retrained faculty; Indonesia would face a sharper version, and the quality gap would be invisible for four years until the first cohort graduates.

(7) DATA INFRASTRUCTURE. No standardised, audited, programme-level graduate destination data means no defensible basis for closure decisions and no defence against accusations of arbitrariness or politics.

(8) LEGAL AND PROCEDURAL FRICTION. Closing a programme requires teach-out arrangements for enrolled students, redeployment or termination of lecturers with attendant labour-law exposure, and creates litigation risk from foundations. Indonesia's administrative courts are an available venue for aggrieved yayasan.

(9) NORMATIVE RESISTANCE. Indonesian higher education discourse retains a strong commitment to education as public good, cultural formation and religious learning. Kompas and other outlets have already argued that 'what should be closed is not the prodi' — locating the problem in institutional quality and governance rather than in disciplinary choice. Islamic higher education (PTKIN under the Ministry of Religious Affairs) sits outside Kemdiktisaintek's authority entirely, fragmenting any national campaign.

(10) BUREAUCRATIC CAPACITY AND ATTENTION. Kemdiktisaintek is simultaneously running Diktisaintek Berdampak, performance contracts, curriculum reform, accreditation reform and the free-nutrition-adjacent budget environment. A restructuring campaign of Chinese intensity requires sustained administrative attention over 5+ years and multiple ministerial terms — Indonesia's education policy has changed direction with almost every minister since 2014, which is itself the deepest barrier.
faktor_pembatal_transfer:
STRUCTURAL REASONS THIS TREND WILL NOT ARRIVE IN INDONESIA IN THE SAME FORM, EVER:

(1) DEMOGRAPHIC DIRECTION IS OPPOSITE. China restructures a system that must shrink: births have collapsed from ~18 million (2016) to under 10 million, so the 18-year-old cohort entering university from the mid-2030s will fall by roughly half, and the tertiary participation rate is already ~60%. Culling 20% of programmes is a rational response to guaranteed future contraction. Indonesia's participation rate is ~32% with a still-large youth cohort; its central problem is that too few young people reach university, not that too many programmes exist. A Chinese-style cull applied to Indonesia would be the right medicine for the wrong disease. This is the single strongest cancellation factor and it does not weaken until roughly the 2040s.

(2) THE INSTRUMENT REQUIRES A STATE-OWNED SYSTEM. China's mechanism is enrolment-quota control plus a closed national catalogue plus direct funding of the affected institutions. Indonesia's private-foundation system is structurally immune to all three. Absent constitutional-scale change in how private higher education is governed and financed, the mechanism cannot be transplanted; only its rhetoric can.

(3) NO INDUSTRIAL DEMAND SIGNAL TO ALIGN TO. China's 16 target industries are real, domestically owned, and hiring at scale. Indonesia's advanced-industry employment is dominated by foreign-owned assembly and by extraction/midstream processing, which demands technicians and operators far more than it demands AI researchers or chip designers. A faithful copy of China's target list would produce programmes whose graduates emigrate or work outside their field — which is what happens today with Indonesian engineering graduates. The correct Indonesian target list is different from the Chinese one, and that difference alone means the trend cannot transfer 'in the same form'.

(4) ARCHIPELAGIC GEOGRAPHY BLOCKS CONSOLIDATION. China can close a weak programme in one city because students can travel to another province. Indonesian students in Maluku, NTT, Papua or interior Kalimantan often cannot substitute a closed local programme with a distant one at any affordable cost. Consolidation logic that works on a contiguous landmass fails across 17,000 islands. Any Indonesian version must therefore work through upgrading and networking regional institutions rather than closing them — a fundamentally different policy.

(5) FISCAL ASYMMETRY. China's new majors are backed by state laboratory investment, National Excellence Engineer Academies, and industrial co-funding. Indonesia's education budget is constitutionally 20% of state spending but overwhelmingly committed to basic education and salaries, with higher education thinly funded and now competing against major new social programmes. Indonesia can rename programmes cheaply; it cannot equip them. A restructuring that changes names without changing laboratories produces credential inflation, not capability.

(6) FRAGMENTED AUTHORITY. Islamic higher education sits under the Ministry of Religious Affairs; vocational and secondary education under Kemendikdasmen; health professions programmes are co-governed with the Ministry of Health and professional colleges. No single Indonesian authority can execute a system-wide portfolio decision the way China's Central Education Work Leading Group can. Fragmentation is not a temporary weakness but a designed feature of Indonesian governance.

(7) POLITICAL COST STRUCTURE IS INVERTED. In China, closing a programme costs the state little and demonstrates decisiveness. In Indonesia, closing a programme creates identifiable, organised, locally-rooted losers (a yayasan, its lecturers, a district's only campus) and diffuse, unidentifiable winners. Indonesian democratic politics reliably resolves such asymmetries in favour of the concentrated losers. Expect moratoria on new permits rather than closures of existing ones — the same policy goal achieved through the only politically survivable instrument.

WHAT WILL ARRIVE INSTEAD: a hybrid — aggressive programme creation, rhetorical relevance-testing, integrity-driven closure of failing institutions, gradual D3-to-D4 conversion, and slow attrition of oversupplied programmes through enrolment collapse rather than administrative decision. Enrolment collapse is already the actual mechanism behind Indonesia's 122 closures in 2026, and it will remain the mechanism. The market will do quietly and inefficiently what the Chinese state does loudly and efficiently.
tahun_masuk_indonesia: ALREADY ENTERING — 2025-2026 is the entry window, in soft form. Markers already observed: 122 study programmes closed during 2026; the ministry publicly discussing programme relevance and 'transformation'; the teacher-education oversupply becoming a national political issue (April-May 2026); UI's S1 AI approved October 2025 for a 2026 intake; UNIKOM's robotics and AI programme from 2025/2026; the Employer Forum in June 2026 demanding radical curriculum reform; 84 private institutions flagged for licence revocation. The idea and the vocabulary have arrived; the instrument has not. FORMAL POLICY ENTRY — the point at which Indonesia adopts an explicit, targeted programme-restructuring policy — is estimated at 2028-2030, most plausibly triggered by a further rise in graduate unemployment or by a fiscal shock to the private sector. [uncertain — depends on ministerial continuity, which has been poor]
tahun_mainstream_indonesia: 2029-2032. By 'mainstream' meaning: most large public and mid-size private universities routinely evaluate and retire programmes on outcome criteria; a national framework exists linking permits or accreditation to graduate placement; AI/data/robotics/energy programmes are standard at 50+ institutions rather than a handful; and D3 business/administration programmes have largely disappeared. Sub-timings: standardised programme-level tracer data mandated ~2028-2029; moratorium on new permits in oversupplied families (teacher education, generic management) ~2028-2030 — likely the first hard instrument Indonesia actually uses; AI/robotics/data programmes at 50+ institutions ~2029-2030; annual closure volume exceeding 500 programmes ~2030-2032. Note the sequencing differs from China's: Indonesia will mainstream the CREATION side around 2028-2029 and the DESTRUCTION side, if at all, around 2031-2033. [uncertain]
tahun_puncak_indonesia: 2033-2038, and shaped by demography rather than by policy. Indonesia's total fertility rate has fallen to roughly 2.1 and continues declining; the cohort entering university in the mid-2030s will be the first to stop growing. That is when Indonesian private higher education faces the same enrolment contraction that made China's cull inevitable, and when closure becomes structurally unavoidable rather than politically optional. A secondary, earlier peak of activity is likely around 2030-2032 if graduate unemployment continues rising and a reform-minded minister with a full term takes it on. The peak will be geographically concentrated in Java (where the density of small private institutions is highest and where inter-institution substitution is feasible) and will manifest as institutional mergers and closures more than as programme-level surgery. If Indonesia's demographic transition proceeds faster than currently projected, pull all these dates forward by 3-5 years. [uncertain — long-horizon projection]
skenario_percepatan: Accelerators, roughly by force: (1) a sustained rise in graduate unemployment above ~8% for D4/S1+, which would convert a technocratic issue into an electoral one; (2) a demographic or economic shock that collapses private-university enrolment, forcing consolidation from below — the most likely real accelerator; (3) an AI-driven contraction in white-collar entry hiring in Indonesia mirroring China's -22% graduate posting shock, which would delegitimise generic business and administration degrees within one admissions cycle; (4) large-scale Chinese or other FDI in advanced manufacturing (batteries, EV, electronics, semiconductors) creating visible, well-paid demand for specific skills, making rotation attractive rather than coercive; (5) a minister with a full five-year term who makes programme relevance a signature agenda and survives a cabinet reshuffle; (6) mandatory, published, programme-level tracer data, which would make the oversupply undeniable and mechanically generate closure pressure; (7) fiscal pressure that forces the state to ration higher education subsidy by programme; (8) a high-visibility scandal — mass unemployment of graduates from a specific programme family, or a diploma-mill collapse — that supplies political cover.
dampak_lapangan_kerja:
JOBS DESTROYED OR DEVALUED
- University lecturers in the cut fields. This is the most direct and least discussed effect. In China, revocation of thousands of programme points forced mass faculty redeployment (转岗): lecturers were moved to adjacent majors, pushed into teaching general/public foundation courses, transferred to administrative, laboratory or library posts, made student counsellors, or left for other institutions. Reports describe teachers 'looking for classes to teach' after 5,345 programme points were revoked. Humanities faculty are additionally disadvantaged in dynamic programme evaluations because the metrics (innovation competitions, 'Internet+' contests, patent and project counts) are engineering-weighted. In Indonesia the equivalent exposure sits with lecturers in ~6,844 education programmes, plus generic management, communications and D3 business faculties — a population in the tens of thousands, disproportionately non-PhD, disproportionately at private institutions with weak labour protection, and disproportionately outside Java.
- Administrative and support staff at institutions that shrink or merge.
- Downstream: the teaching profession itself becomes a rationed occupation. ~490,000 Indonesian teacher-education graduates a year against ~20,000 vacancies means the degree already functions as a consumption good rather than a labour-market credential; formalising that recognition destroys the implicit job promise that sustained enrolment.
- Test-prep, admissions consulting and private tutoring built around now-devalued programmes.

JOBS CHANGED
- Every lecturer in a surviving programme faces curriculum rewrite obligations: China's 2025-2027 Action Plan explicitly requires accelerated content iteration and AI-empowered teaching, meaning the job of 'teaching a stable syllabus for a decade' ends. Indonesia's Wamendiktisaintek made the same demand at the June 2026 Employer Forum.
- Career-services and industry-liaison roles move from peripheral to central, because graduate placement becomes the metric that determines programme survival.
- Institutional research, tracer-study and data roles become mandatory infrastructure.
- Accreditation and quality-assurance professionals gain leverage; in Indonesia, BAN-PT and the LAMs become the chokepoint.

JOBS CREATED
- Faculty and technical staff in the new fields: AI, machine learning, robotics, embodied intelligence, chip and integrated-circuit design, battery and energy-systems engineering, drone/low-altitude systems, carbon accounting and climate engineering, bioprocess engineering. China's 621 AI programmes alone imply tens of thousands of teaching posts.
- Laboratory technicians, simulation and equipment specialists, industry-embedded instructors — the National Excellence Engineer Academy model in China, the Center of Excellence and link-and-match model in Indonesia.
- Curriculum designers, EdTech and courseware developers for the new fields, and corporate-academy staff at firms that build their own pipelines (Huawei ICT Academy pattern).
- Retraining providers for displaced faculty — a market that barely exists in Indonesia and will need to.

THE CENTRAL CAVEAT: China's own data suggests the new jobs promise is oversold at the student level — only ~55% of 2024 AI graduates entered field-relevant work, and about half judged their curriculum outdated. Restructuring reallocates the mismatch rather than eliminating it unless the receiving industry is real. Indonesia's receiving industry is thinner than China's, so the Indonesian version will create fewer genuine graduate-level jobs per programme opened, while still destroying faculty jobs in the programmes it closes. The net employment effect in Indonesia is likely negative in the short run and positive only if industrial policy delivers actual employers.
dampak_kelas_menengah:
Higher education is the primary technology of middle-class reproduction in Indonesia, so restructuring hits the middle class more directly than almost any other trend in this research set.

(1) THE DEGREE AS INSURANCE STOPS WORKING. The Indonesian middle-class bargain — pay for a bachelor's degree, receive a white-collar job — is already fraying, with D4/S1+ unemployment at 6.13% (Feb 2026) and rising from 5.38% three months earlier. Restructuring makes the failure explicit and official: when the state says a programme is 'not relevant', it retroactively devalues the credentials of everyone who already holds it. In China this produced open discussion of 'trap majors' (天坑专业) and of humanities graduates facing 7:1 supply-demand ratios; Indonesia's version will be sharper because Indonesian middle-class families carry more of the cost privately (tuition at private institutions, plus living costs) with far less state subsidy than Chinese families.

(2) THE COST OF CHOOSING WRONG RISES, AND FALLS HARDEST ON THE INFORMATIONALLY POOR. Upper-middle-class families in Jakarta, Surabaya and Bandung read the signals early, hire consultants, and route children to AI, computing, medicine or overseas study. Lower-middle-class families in secondary cities receive the signal late, through TikTok, and after their child has already enrolled. Restructuring therefore widens intra-middle-class stratification — the same dynamic China's gaokao advisory industry produced, where AI major cut-off scores rose sharply while humanities scores fell.

(3) THE LECTURER STRATUM IS DIRECTLY THREATENED. University lecturers are a core Indonesian middle-class occupation, especially outside Java where a private campus is often one of the few white-collar employers in a district. Programme closure converts secure middle-class professionals into displaced workers with narrow, non-transferable specialisation. In China this was managed through redeployment inside state-funded institutions; Indonesia's private sector offers no such cushion.

(4) THE YAYASAN OWNER CLASS FACES ASSET DESTRUCTION. Small private universities are middle-class family assets. A restructuring regime, or simply enrolment collapse, wipes out that capital.

(5) A COUNTERVAILING POSITIVE. For middle-class students who do land in genuinely well-built new programmes with real employers attached, restructuring is straightforwardly good: it is the difference between a marketing degree with no employer and a battery-engineering degree with three. The middle-class gain from this trend is real but narrow, concentrated in perhaps 15-20 institutions, and it will be captured disproportionately by those already advantaged.

(6) SECOND-ORDER: MIDDLE-CLASS FAITH IN EDUCATION AS MOBILITY. If the degree stops guaranteeing mobility, middle-class investment behaviour shifts — toward vocational certification, overseas study, entrepreneurship, or simply lower fertility and delayed family formation. China is already visibly experiencing all four. This is the mechanism by which an education-policy item becomes a demographic and consumption item, connecting directly to the Consumer Downgrade and Youth Unemployment items in this research set.
dampak_daerah_non_jawa:
THIS IS WHERE INDONESIA DIVERGES MOST SHARPLY FROM CHINA, AND WHERE THE RISK IS HIGHEST.

(1) THE CLOSURE BURDEN FALLS OUTSIDE JAVA AND OUTSIDE THE ELITE. The programmes most vulnerable to any relevance test — small D3 programmes, teacher education, generic management, low-enrolment science programmes at under-resourced institutions — are concentrated in secondary cities and outside Java. Java-based flagship institutions have the enrolment, endowment and accreditation to survive any test. A national restructuring campaign therefore functions as a regional redistribution against the outer islands, unless deliberately designed otherwise. China observed exactly this: cutting was heaviest in provincial and second-tier institutions in Jiangxi, Anhui, Henan and Shandong, while new major creation concentrated in Beijing, Shanghai, Jiangsu, Guangdong and Zhejiang.

(2) THE CREATION BENEFIT ALSO FALLS TO JAVA. UI's AI programme is in Depok; the faculty, laboratories, industry partners and venture ecosystem needed for AI, robotics and semiconductor programmes exist almost exclusively in Greater Jakarta, Bandung, Surabaya and Yogyakarta. Without deliberate intervention, restructuring simultaneously subtracts from the periphery and adds to the core — a double concentration.

(3) ACCESS IS NOT SUBSTITUTABLE ACROSS WATER. A student in Sumba, Maluku or interior Papua whose local programme closes does not enrol elsewhere; they exit higher education. With national gross participation at ~32% and far lower in eastern Indonesia, closure translates directly into lost access, not into reallocation. This is the strongest argument against importing the Chinese instrument wholesale, and it is a geographic fact that no policy design can wish away.

(4) BUT THERE IS A GENUINE REGIONAL OPPORTUNITY THAT CHINA'S MODEL POINTS TO. China's most transferable idea is not the cull — it is the regional matching pilot: since 2024, eight provinces have aligned programme portfolios to local 100-billion- and trillion-yuan industrial clusters, building 247 'characteristic advantage major clusters'. Indonesia's equivalent is obvious and mostly unbuilt: nickel/battery metallurgy and industrial automation programmes in Central and North Sulawesi (Morowali, Weda Bay), marine and fisheries technology plus port logistics in Maluku and NTT, geothermal and renewables engineering in North Sumatra and NTT, oil palm and biomass process engineering in Riau and Kalimantan, tourism and creative industries in Bali and NTB, and coal-transition and reclamation engineering in East Kalimantan and South Sumatra. Each of these is a regional industry with real employers that currently imports its technical workforce from Java or abroad while the local university teaches management and education. A regionally-matched Indonesian version of the Chinese policy would ADD capacity outside Java rather than subtract it, and is the strongest positive recommendation to come out of this comparison.

D3 Midwifery (16), D3 Informatics Management (8), D3 Accounting (7), D3 Computer Engineering (3), D3 Nursing (3), D3 Finance and Banking (3), S1 Retail Management (3), S1 Mathematics (2).

INDONESIA'S EXPOSED LIST — programmes with the structural characteristics that killed their Chinese equivalents:
- TEACHER EDUCATION AND KEPENDIDIKAN, at massive scale: 6,844 programmes, ~490,000 graduates a year against ~20,000 vacancies. Highest-volume risk in the entire Indonesian system. Note the important nuance: the problem is quantity and distribution, not the discipline — Indonesia genuinely needs teachers, it does not need 490,000 new ones a year from programmes of uneven quality.
- All remaining D3 programmes in business, administration, accounting, secretarial studies, informatics management and banking — being displaced by D4/vocational bachelor's degrees, and separately by automation of the clerical work they feed.
- GENERIC MANAGEMENT AND BUSINESS ADMINISTRATION at institutions with no industry linkage, no research output and no distinctive specialisation. This is Indonesia's single largest undifferentiated block after teacher education.
- Communications, Public Relations, Advertising, Broadcasting — where generative AI is compressing entry-level production work fastest.
- Library and Information Science, Office Administration, generic Information Systems.
- Non-clinical health support programmes at diploma level where scope-of-practice has moved to D4.
- Generic Design (graphic, product, fashion) at non-elite institutions — mirroring China's Product Design and Apparel Design cuts, and now compounded by generative image tools.
- Minor foreign languages and literature programmes at institutions with tiny cohorts — though see the caveat below.
- Basic sciences (Mathematics, Physics, Chemistry, Biology) at institutions lacking laboratories: note S1 Mathematics already appears on Indonesia's 2026 closure list, which is a warning sign, because China's 2025-2027 Action Plan explicitly added a counterweight action to PROTECT basic disciplines after over-cutting them. Indonesia risks repeating China's mistake without China's corrective.

IMPORTANT CAVEATS, STATED DELIBERATELY:
(a) The threat is to the PROGRAMME AS CURRENTLY TAUGHT, not to the discipline. Marketing did not stop mattering; generic marketing degrees stopped signalling anything. The Chinese cuts fell hardest on programmes that were cheap to open and identical everywhere.
(b) 'Humanities are dying' is the wrong conclusion and China itself is retreating from it. china_education_response:
THIS ITEM IS ITSELF THE CHINESE EDUCATION RESPONSE — the education system's answer to AI, automation, industrial upgrading and graduate unemployment, executed through the degree catalogue. Its full architecture:

(1) LEGAL/ADMINISTRATIVE ARCHITECTURE. A binding national undergraduate major catalogue (883 majors, 92 major classes, 13 degree categories as of 2026), revised annually, with every programme point at every institution requiring registration or ministerial approval. This is the instrument that makes everything else possible and that Indonesia does not have.

(2) THE QUOTA. February 2023, five ministries: optimise/adjust ~20% of national discipline-major setting points by 2025. Delivered >30% cumulative churn — 10,200 added, 12,200 revoked or suspended, with the 2025 single-year ratio at 10.1%.

(3) THE ESCALATION. 28 August 2025, Central Education Work Leading Group, Action Plan 2025-2027, with six action lines: extraordinary/fast-track layout of urgently needed disciplines; strengthening of basic disciplines (the explicit counterweight to over-cutting); incubation of emerging and interdisciplinary fields including demonstration interdisciplinary centres; optimisation of existing programmes with formal warnings and mandated remediation where social demand, training quality or conditions are inadequate; curriculum content modernisation with AI-empowered teaching; and training-model reform through National Excellence Engineer Academies.

(4) THE INDUSTRIAL ALIGNMENT. MOE notice of 30 June 2025 directing programme setting at 16 named industry fields. Since 2024, eight provinces run a pilot matching programme portfolios to regional industrial clusters, producing 247 'characteristic advantage major clusters' tied to 100-billion- and trillion-yuan regional industries.

(5) THE EXIT MECHANISM. Provincial employment-based red/yellow cards: Jiangxi issues a yellow card and cuts enrolment quota below a 50% graduate destination rate, a red card and enrolment suspension after two consecutive years below 50%; Anhui and Jiangxi revoke after 2-3 consecutive years below 60%. Jiangxi's five-year net: +312 programme points, -335 stopped or revoked. Fujian and Jiangxi pioneered the mechanism from 2022; it is now widespread.

(6) THE FAST-TRACK CREATION MECHANISM. 'Extraordinary' (超常规) approval for strategically urgent majors, bypassing the normal cycle — used for Low-Altitude Technology and Engineering (6 universities, 2025) and Embodied Intelligence (9 universities, 2026). China can now go from national priority to first student intake in roughly 12-18 months, which is the real capability being demonstrated.

(7) THE STRUCTURAL INNOVATION. The 2026 catalogue created a thirteenth top-level degree category, Interdisciplinary (交叉学科), populated with Future Robotics, Interdisciplinary Engineering, Embodied Intelligence and Brain-Computer Science and Technology, and explicitly designed to connect the undergraduate and postgraduate discipline catalogues. This is the deepest change: China stopped forcing new fields into old faculty boundaries.

(8) THE ELITE-INSTITUTION SIGNAL. Fudan capping humanities and social sciences at 20% of undergraduate intake under 'refine the humanities, sharpen the sciences, strengthen engineering, renew medicine, enliven the interdisciplinary', delivering an almost exactly 20/20/20/20/20 class in 2025.

(9) THE VOCATIONAL PARALLEL. 27 new vocational majors in 2026 (AI, low-altitude economy, humanoid robotics, first intake 2027), ~40 in the prior cycle, 33 new undergraduate-level vocational colleges approved with roughly half upgraded from vocational schools, a target of vocational undergraduate places at ≥10% of vocational higher education enrolment by 2025, and a 2022 legal revision giving vocational education parity with general education — all responding to a projected ~30 million skilled-worker shortage.

(10) THE SELF-CORRECTION ALREADY UNDERWAY. Chinese official and academic discourse now openly discusses the herd-behaviour problem (institutions opening AI programmes without faculty, laboratories or curriculum, sometimes by prefixing 'intelligent' to an existing major name), the outcome problem (only ~55% of 2024 AI graduates in field-relevant work; about half calling their curriculum outdated), the faculty-displacement problem, and the basic-disciplines problem. The 2025-2027 Action Plan's second action line exists because of the third of these. Indonesia's most valuable takeaway is not the cull but this correction: China is telling the world, in advance, which parts of the policy fail.

TRANSFERABLE VS NON-TRANSFERABLE: the mechanism (catalogue + quota + kill switch) is not transferable to Indonesia's private-dominant system. The DIAGNOSTIC APPARATUS is fully transferable and cheap — programme-level graduate destination data, published, comparable, annual. The REGIONAL MATCHING PILOT is transferable and desirable. The FAST-TRACK CREATION PROCEDURE is transferable and would fix Indonesia's slowest bottleneck. The FUDAN-STYLE HUMANITIES CAP is transferable but should not be copied.
respons_kebijakan_china:
CHINA'S CORRECTIVE AND GUARD-RAIL POLICIES — the regulations imposed after the campaign started producing damage, which are the ones Indonesia should adopt preemptively:

(1) EXPLICIT PROTECTION OF BASIC DISCIPLINES. The 2025-2027 Action Plan's second action line strengthens basic disciplines inside excellence-building schemes — an admission that outcome-driven cutting had endangered mathematics, physics, chemistry, biology and core humanities, which have long payback periods and poor short-run employment metrics. LESSON FOR INDONESIA: ring-fence basic sciences and core humanities from any relevance test BEFORE the test is created, not after. Indonesia has already closed S1 Mathematics programmes in 2026 without such a guard-rail in place.

(2) FACULTY TRANSITION RIGHTS AND REDEPLOYMENT PATHWAYS. Chinese universities were required to build teacher-transition provisions into their own programme-adjustment regulations. Documented practice at one Hunan institution offers five redeployment tracks: teaching posts in adjacent programmes within the same school, other technical posts, administrative posts, student-counsellor posts, and posts in the innovation and entrepreneurship college. Experts additionally recommend visiting-scholar opportunities, a defined 'buffer zone' for transitioning teachers, and broadened evaluation systems so that teaching-track and teaching-research-track careers are viable. LESSON FOR INDONESIA: no programme closure regulation without a mandatory, funded lecturer transition scheme — otherwise closure means unemployment for a middle-class professional group with no cushion in the private sector.

(3) TEACH-OUT PROTECTION FOR ENROLLED STUDENTS. The Chinese distinction between 停招 (suspend new enrolment) and 撤销 (revoke) exists precisely so that enrolled cohorts complete their degrees; the standard sequence is warning, then enrolment suspension with a remediation period, then revocation. LESSON FOR INDONESIA: legislate the sequence — warning, remediation window, enrolment suspension, closure — never immediate termination, and guarantee transfer rights.

(4) WARNING BEFORE EXECUTION. Chinese provinces issue yellow cards with quota deductions before red cards with suspension, and the national Action Plan requires warnings plus improvement requirements rather than direct closure. LESSON FOR INDONESIA: build a graduated, published, appealable warning ladder — this also creates the political cover that makes closure survivable.

(5) MULTI-CRITERIA EVALUATION, NOT EMPLOYMENT RATE ALONE. The Action Plan's fourth line triggers on three criteria — insufficient social demand, declining training quality, AND inadequate conditions — not on employment rate alone. Chinese critics note that evaluation metrics weighted toward engineering-style outputs systematically disadvantage humanities faculty. LESSON FOR INDONESIA: never build a single-metric kill switch; a graduate-employment-only rule would be gamed instantly and would destroy disciplines whose value is not captured by first-job placement.

(6) REGIONAL MATCHING RATHER THAN UNIFORM NATIONAL TARGETS. The eight-province pilot aligning programmes to local industrial clusters (247 clusters) is the part of the Chinese design most suited to a diverse, decentralised country. LESSON FOR INDONESIA: any Indonesian version should be provincial and cluster-based from day one — nickel/battery in Sulawesi, marine in eastern Indonesia, geothermal in Sumatra — not a uniform Jakarta-issued percentage.

(7) CONTROLLING HERD BEHAVIOUR IN NEW PROGRAMME APPROVAL. China's most-criticised failure: hundreds of institutions opened AI programmes without adequate faculty, laboratories or curriculum, some merely renaming existing majors, producing only ~55% field-relevant employment for 2024 AI graduates. China's answer has been fast-track approval reserved for capable institutions plus conditions-based review. LESSON FOR INDONESIA — THE MOST URGENT ONE: gate new AI/robotics/semiconductor programme permits on verified faculty qualifications, laboratory capacity and named industry partners. Indonesia is at exactly the moment before this mistake, and can avoid it at zero cost.

(8) VOCATIONAL PARITY IN LAW. China's 2022 Vocational Education Law revision gave vocational education legal parity with general education, plus undergraduate-level vocational institutions. LESSON FOR INDONESIA: elevate applied/vocational bachelor's degrees in law, funding and civil-service recruitment rules, so that D4/vocational pathways become a destination rather than a consolation.

(9) MANDATORY, COMPARABLE, PUBLISHED OUTCOME DATA. The whole Chinese system runs on annual graduate destination rates per programme point. LESSON FOR INDONESIA: this is the cheapest, highest-leverage, least politically costly reform available, and it should come first — transparency will drive most of the adjustment through student choice before any closure power is ever needed.

(10) CURRICULUM ITERATION AS A STANDING OBLIGATION. The Action Plan's fifth line mandates accelerated content iteration and AI-empowered teaching across all programmes. LESSON FOR INDONESIA: the higher-return intervention is usually reforming what is taught inside an existing programme, not deleting the programme.

12. Explicitly EXEMPT institutions that are the sole tertiary provider in their district from closure pressure, replacing closure with mandatory partnership, franchising of curriculum from stronger institutions, and shared-faculty arrangements.

CROSS-CUTTING
