peluang_bisnis:
(1) LECTURER AND FACULTY RESKILLING — the clearest under-served market. Tens of thousands of Indonesian lecturers in oversupplied fields need credible retraining into adjacent teachable areas (data literacy, applied AI, industry-linked pedagogy). China ran this through state institutions; Indonesia has no dominant provider. Addressable via micro-credentials, industry certification partnerships, and cohort-based programmes sold to yayasan and to LLDIKTI. Demand is guaranteed by the arithmetic regardless of whether closures happen.

(2) TURNKEY PROGRAMME-IN-A-BOX FOR NEW MAJORS. Most Indonesian institutions want an AI, data, robotics or renewable-energy programme and cannot build one: no curriculum, no faculty, no laboratory, no industry partner. A packaged offering — accredited curriculum, laboratory specification and equipment, trained instructors, industry placement network, capstone project pipeline — sold per programme is a high-margin, sticky business. This is exactly the gap that produced China's herd-behaviour quality failure, which means the market will exist and the quality bar will be the differentiator. Adjacent: laboratory equipment supply and integration (robotics cells, embedded systems, power electronics, microfabrication teaching kits), where Chinese vendors will compete aggressively on price.

(3) GRADUATE OUTCOME DATA AND TRACER-STUDY INFRASTRUCTURE. If Indonesia mandates programme-level outcome reporting — the most likely first policy move — every institution needs instrumentation. Tracer-study platforms, alumni CRM, employer feedback systems, and analytics benchmarking a programme against national peers. Sells to institutions on compliance and to the ministry as national infrastructure. Small market today, mandatory market within three years.

(4) INDEPENDENT PROGRAMME RATINGS AND CAREER-OUTCOME GUIDANCE FOR FAMILIES. Indonesian families are making six-figure-rupiah-per-semester decisions with almost no outcome information. China's gaokao advisory industry is large and profitable. An Indonesian equivalent — programme-level ROI data, honest employability ratings, admissions advisory — has strong consumer demand and a clean media/subscription/lead-generation model. Ethical risk to manage: this business profits from fear.

(5) INSTITUTIONAL TURNAROUND AND M&A ADVISORY. With 84 private institutions flagged for possible licence revocation and structural consolidation coming, there is a professional services market in merger advisory, portfolio restructuring, accreditation remediation and distressed-asset transactions for yayasan — a market that essentially does not exist in Indonesia today.

(6) INDUSTRY-EMBEDDED ACADEMIES AND APPRENTICESHIP INTERMEDIATION. Employers in nickel/battery, EV assembly, electronics, renewables and digital services need technicians and engineers that universities do not produce. A firm that builds and operates corporate academies, or that intermediates structured apprenticeships between industrial estates and regional campuses, monetises the mismatch directly rather than waiting for universities to fix it. Strongest in Morowali, Weda Bay, Karawang-Cikarang, Batam and Gresik.

(7) ALTERNATIVE CREDENTIALS FOR THE DISPLACED. If the degree signal weakens as it has in China, demand shifts to shorter, employer-recognised credentials: bootcamps with verified placement, professional certifications, and portfolio-based assessment. The Indonesian bootcamp sector has already been through one hype cycle and a shakeout; the surviving model is employer-paid or income-share with genuine placement, not consumer-paid hope.

(8) SPECIALIST NICHE INSTITUTIONS. The Chinese pattern rewards differentiation and punishes generic provision. A small, focused, expensive Indonesian institution in one defensible field — battery and electrochemical engineering, marine technology, agritech, or health technology — with real industry ownership, is a more durable asset than a generic multi-faculty private university. Effectively, applying the Chinese lesson at the level of a single firm.

(9) EDTECH FOR CURRICULUM ITERATION. If curriculum must be updated continuously, institutions need tooling: courseware that updates, assessment banks, simulation and virtual laboratories (which also solve the equipment-cost problem for regional campuses), and AI teaching assistants. Virtual laboratories are especially well matched to an archipelagic country where equipment cannot be replicated everywhere.

(10) THE CONTRARIAN PLAY. When everyone rotates into AI, the scarce assets become the ones being abandoned: qualified mathematics and statistics teaching, laboratory-grade basic science, language and area-studies expertise, and skilled trades instruction. China's own corrective — adding a basic-disciplines action line after over-cutting — suggests these recover. Building capability in what is currently being discarded is a five-to-ten-year position with little competition.
rekomendasi_individu_mahasiswa:
(1) CHOOSE THE INSTITUTION AND THE EVIDENCE, NOT THE PROGRAMME NAME. China's clearest lesson: 621 institutions offer AI, only ~55% of 2024 AI graduates found field-relevant work, and half called their curriculum outdated. A weak AI programme is worse than a strong mathematics programme. Before enrolling, demand evidence: how many faculty hold PhDs in the actual field, what laboratory exists, which employers hire from this programme, where did last year's graduates go. If the institution cannot answer, the programme is a name change.

(2) IF YOU ARE ALREADY IN A THREATENED PROGRAMME, DO NOT PANIC AND DO NOT TRANSFER REFLEXIVELY. Finish the degree — enrolled cohorts are protected in every closure regime — and build the complement rather than replacing the base. A teacher-education student who adds instructional design, EdTech and data skills is more employable than a mediocre computer science graduate. Marketing plus analytics, law plus technology regulation, communications plus AI-assisted production, design plus generative tooling: the pattern that survives is domain knowledge plus computational capability, and it beats both pure options.

(3) BUILD THE THREE THINGS THAT SURVIVE EVERY RESTRUCTURING. Quantitative reasoning (statistics and basic programming, whatever your field). Working fluency with AI tools as a collaborator, not a novelty — this is now mandated across the curriculum in China and will be assumed by Indonesian employers within three years. And demonstrated output: a portfolio, shipped projects, real internships. When degree signals weaken, portfolios become the signal.

(4) TARGET INDONESIA'S ACTUAL COMPARATIVE ADVANTAGES, NOT CHINA'S. Copying China's target list is a mistake: Indonesia has no domestic quantum industry and no eVTOL manufacturing base. Indonesia does have the world's largest nickel resource and a growing battery chain, an enormous marine and fisheries economy, a large agricultural sector ripe for technology, geothermal potential, a young digital consumer market, and a globally significant carbon and biodiversity asset base. Battery and electrochemical engineering, marine and aquaculture technology, agritech, geothermal and renewables, carbon and environmental measurement, and applied AI on top of any of these are fields where an Indonesian graduate can be globally relevant rather than a second-rate copy of a Chinese graduate.

(5) TAKE THE VOCATIONAL/APPLIED ROUTE SERIOUSLY. China legislated vocational parity and is expanding vocational bachelor's degrees against a projected 30-million skilled-worker shortage. Indonesia's industrial estates and processing plants have the same shortage today. A D4 or applied engineering qualification with real plant experience frequently out-earns a generic S1, and this gap will widen.

(6) LANGUAGES: MOVE UP THE VALUE CHAIN, DO NOT ABANDON. Routine translation is finished. But China created Area Studies, International Communication, International Law and International Organisations majors precisely as language study moved upward. Mandarin plus a technical or legal or commercial specialisation is a genuinely scarce Indonesian combination, especially with Chinese industrial investment concentrated in Indonesia.

(7) FOR HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCE STUDENTS SPECIFICALLY. Do not accept the 'useless major' narrative uncritically — even China is correcting it. But do accept that generic provision is being devalued, and respond by specialising into something scarce: technology policy, AI ethics, computational social science, digital heritage, area studies, or research and evaluation methods. The Indonesian public sector, civil society and international organisations demand exactly these and cannot fill the roles.

(8) WATCH THE INSTITUTION'S SOLVENCY, NOT ONLY ITS RANKING. With 84 private institutions flagged for possible licence revocation, enrolling at a financially fragile campus is a real risk to your credential. Check accreditation status, enrolment trend and whether the institution has closed programmes recently.

(9) ASSUME A 40-YEAR CAREER WITH FOUR RESKILLINGS. Every specific technical skill taught today has a shorter half-life than your working life. The durable investments are learning capability, statistical and causal reasoning, writing and argument, and professional networks. Chinese graduates who over-optimised for a hot major in 2019 are discovering this in 2026.
rekomendasi_perguruan_tinggi:
OPEN, WITH INPUT GATES ENFORCED FROM DAY ONE: applied AI and machine learning engineering; data engineering; cybersecurity; battery, electrochemical and metallurgical process engineering; renewable energy systems and geothermal engineering; industrial automation and mechatronics; agritech, food technology and aquaculture/marine technology; logistics and port engineering; applied statistics and actuarial science; semiconductor and microelectronics engineering (at the 5-8 institutions capable of it); biotechnology and bioinformatics; carbon accounting, climate risk and environmental engineering; geospatial and remote-sensing engineering; drone/UAV systems for agriculture, logistics and maritime surveillance — Indonesia's realistic version of China's 'low-altitude economy'; and on the humanities side, area and country studies, international and trade law, technology policy and AI ethics, and computational social science.

TRANSFORM RATHER THAN CLOSE (the higher-return move, and consistent with the minister's own framing): generic management → operations analytics, supply chain, or sector-specific management with a named industry; accounting → data-driven audit, forensic accounting and sustainability reporting; communications/PR → AI-assisted content production, strategic and international communication; generic design → creative technology, UX/service design, digital heritage; information systems → data engineering or cybersecurity; electrical engineering → power electronics, energy systems or robotics tracks (the example the minister himself uses); teacher education → subject-specialist teacher preparation with instructional design and EdTech, at drastically reduced intake.

CONSOLIDATE AND SHRINK INTAKE, NOT NECESSARILY CLOSE: teacher education, where the correct policy is a large intake reduction plus a quality floor plus mandatory placement pathways, not deletion of 6,844 programmes; remaining D3 business and administration programmes, converting to D4; and small basic-science programmes, which should be networked and shared across institutions rather than closed — China's need to add a basic-disciplines counterweight is the warning here.

CURRICULUM CHANGES ACROSS ALL PROGRAMMES, REGARDLESS OF FIELD: AI literacy and AI-assisted workflow as a required component in every degree (this is China's system-wide mandate and the single highest-return change); statistics and data reasoning for non-STEM students; a mandatory industry or field project with an external assessor; portfolio-based assessment alongside examinations; and a formal curriculum iteration cycle with a maximum content age, because the failure mode Chinese AI students report is a curriculum that is already obsolete at graduation.

INSTITUTIONAL GOVERNANCE MOVES: publish programme-level graduate outcomes voluntarily, before it is mandated — it will become a competitive advantage; create a faculty transition fund and redeployment policy before any programme is touched; differentiate rather than replicate, because the Chinese cull fell hardest on programmes that were identical everywhere; build one or two defensible specialisations tied to the institution's regional industry instead of a full generic faculty spread; and for regional institutions, form consortia to share scarce faculty and expensive laboratories, plus virtual laboratory infrastructure, so that geography stops being a reason for low quality.

WHAT NOT TO DO: do not open an AI or robotics programme without qualified faculty, a laboratory and named industry partners — this is precisely the mistake China made at scale and is now publicly criticising, and Indonesia can avoid it for free. Do not rename a programme and call it transformation. Do not cut basic sciences and core humanities to chase employment metrics. And do not adopt a percentage target for closures.
dampak_negatif_china:
(1) FACULTY DISPLACEMENT AND CAREER DESTRUCTION. Thousands of lecturers whose programmes were revoked have been redeployed into adjacent majors, general foundation courses, administration, laboratories, libraries or counsellor posts — or have left. Reporting describes teachers 'looking for classes to teach' in the wake of 5,345 revoked programme points. Humanities faculty fare worst, because dynamic programme evaluation weights engineering-style outputs (innovation competitions, 'Internet+' contests, projects) that humanities departments cannot generate. A generation of mid-career academics in soft disciplines has had its professional identity administratively invalidated.

(2) STUDENTS STRANDED IN DYING PROGRAMMES. Students enrolled in a programme that is suspended or revoked complete a degree that the state has publicly declared obsolete. The harm is documented as occurring both during study (declining resources, departing faculty, demoralised departments) and at job-seeking time, when the programme's public devaluation attaches to the graduate. This is the cost of a policy that changes the value of a credential after it has been purchased.

(3) HERD BEHAVIOUR AND QUALITY COLLAPSE IN THE NEW PROGRAMMES. 621 institutions opened AI majors by 2024 — the most-added major of the decade. Chinese commentary is now blunt about the result: ordinary institutions opened AI programmes to ride the trend without disciplinary strength; faculty were the original staff 'learning while teaching'; curricula were generic; some institutions simply prefixed 'intelligent' to an existing major name; teaching materials could not keep pace with large-model development. Outcome: only ~55% of 2024 AI undergraduate graduates entered field-relevant work and about half judged the curriculum impractical or outdated. The policy has begun manufacturing a new mismatch while dismantling the old one. Commentary now warns that AI may become the next 'trap major' (天坑专业).

(4) MARGINALISATION OF THE HUMANITIES AND A NARROWING OF THE NATIONAL INTELLECTUAL BASE. Fudan's cap at 20% was widely read as the definitive signal that humanities are being pushed to the periphery at exactly the institutions best equipped to teach them well. The consequences — thinner critical scholarship, weaker area studies, less capacity for social self-understanding — are real, slow, and invisible in any employment metric. China's own corrective action line on basic disciplines is an admission that outcome-driven cutting cut too deep.

(5) DISTORTED APPLICATION BEHAVIOUR AND A SCORE ARMS RACE. High-scoring applicants pile into AI programmes, cut-offs rise, and students who would have thrived in other fields are funnelled into one. The signalling cascade — universities open, applicants pile in, scores rise, more universities open — is a classic bubble structure, and it is running now.

(6) REGIONAL AND INSTITUTIONAL INEQUALITY WIDENED. Cutting concentrated in second- and third-tier provincial institutions; creation concentrated in the elite coastal cluster. The gap between a Beijing/Shanghai/Guangdong degree and a provincial one widened during a period when China was nominally pursuing common prosperity.

(7) EMPLOYMENT-RATE GAMING. When graduate destination rate below 50% suspends a programme and below 60% for 2-3 years revokes it, institutions have an existential incentive to manipulate the number. Reports of coerced or fabricated employment agreements have circulated in Chinese media for years. A metric that determines survival stops measuring anything.

(8) THE POLICY MAY BE TREATING A SYMPTOM. The 2026 graduate cohort of 12.7 million faces roughly 5.67 million campus recruitment posts and youth unemployment near 16%. No rearrangement of the degree catalogue creates jobs; it changes who queues where. There is a real risk that programme restructuring functions as visible action substituting for demand-side policy — and that when the newly minted AI and robotics graduates also fail to find work, the credibility cost falls on the education system.

(9) INSTITUTIONAL WHIPLASH AND SHORT-TERMISM. Adjusting >30% of programme points in five years, with annual catalogue revisions and fast-track approvals, means universities plan on a horizon shorter than a single undergraduate degree. A programme approved in 2025 graduates its first cohort in 2029, into an economy the 2025 plan cannot see.
risiko_sosial_indonesia:
(1) CLOSURE BECOMES ACCESS DESTRUCTION. This is the dominant Indonesian risk. At ~32% gross participation, in an archipelago where students cannot substitute across islands, closing programmes at regional private institutions removes tertiary education entirely for affected students rather than redirecting them. China cut from abundance; Indonesia would cut from scarcity. Executed without geographic exemptions, an Indonesian cull would deepen the Java/non-Java divide more than any other policy in this research set.

(2) CREDENTIAL INFLATION WITHOUT CAPABILITY — THE MOST LIKELY ACTUAL OUTCOME. Because opening programmes is profitable and closing them is not, Indonesia will import the creation half and skip the destruction half. Result: hundreds of AI, data and robotics programmes taught by retrained lecturers without laboratories or industry partners, graduating students whose credential says 'AI engineer' and whose capability does not. Indonesia would then have both the old oversupply AND a new one. China's 55%-field-relevance datapoint is the preview; Indonesia's version would be worse because its faculty base is thinner and its regulatory gating weaker.

(3) MASS DEVALUATION OF EXISTING GRADUATES. Roughly 490,000 teacher-education graduates a year, plus large cohorts in generic management and communications, are already entering a market that cannot absorb them. An official declaration that their programmes are 'irrelevant' converts a private disappointment into a public humiliation and a political grievance — with an identifiable villain (the ministry) and organised representation (teacher organisations, student groups, campus networks). Indonesia's youth political mobilisation capacity is high and demonstrated.

(4) LECTURER UNEMPLOYMENT WITH NO SAFETY NET. China absorbed displaced faculty inside state-funded institutions. Indonesia's private lecturers have weak tenure, low pay, limited pension coverage and non-transferable specialisation. Closure at scale creates a cohort of unemployed middle-class professionals, concentrated outside Java, with no retraining infrastructure — the exact profile that produces sustained political anger.

(5) INSTITUTIONAL COLLAPSE CASCADE. 84 private institutions flagged for licence revocation, 23-25 already revoked. If enrolment decline compounds with restructuring pressure, the failure mode is disorderly collapse — institutions closing mid-semester, students stranded without transcript portability, transferred credits not recognised. Indonesia has no adequate teach-out or student-protection framework for institutional failure.

(6) ELITE CAPTURE OF THE BENEFITS. New programmes, industry partnerships, laboratory funding and international collaboration will concentrate at 15-20 institutions in Java. Restructuring becomes a mechanism for converting a broad, mediocre system into a narrow, good one plus a large abandoned remainder — with the remainder serving the students with the fewest alternatives.

(7) METRIC GAMING AND CORRUPTION. Any Indonesian employment-rate kill switch will be gamed immediately, and where programme survival depends on an audited number, the incentive to purchase a favourable audit is created. Given documented integrity problems in Indonesian higher education — phantom students, diploma fraud, the 23-25 revoked institutions — introducing a high-stakes metric before fixing data integrity would generate a new corruption market.

(8) ABANDONING FIELDS INDONESIA CANNOT AFFORD TO LOSE. S1 Mathematics already appears on the 2026 closure list. A country with 0.3% R&D intensity that lets its basic-science teaching capacity erode forecloses on any future technological catch-up, because you cannot build semiconductor or AI capability on a base without mathematicians and physicists. The same applies to humanities capacity in a diverse democracy that needs people who can study it.

(9) TEACHER SUPPLY WHIPLASH. Cutting teacher-education intake based on '20,000 vacancies' while another ministry reports a shortage of 679,000 teachers risks solving the wrong problem and producing a genuine teacher shortage a decade later — a slow, severe, hard-to-reverse harm.

(10) POLICY DISCONTINUITY. Indonesian education policy has reversed direction with nearly every ministerial change since 2014. A half-executed restructuring — programmes closed, replacements unfunded, transitions abandoned mid-stream — would be worse than either doing it properly or not doing it at all.
unintended_consequences:
IN CHINA, OBSERVED:
- The rescue programme became the next trap. AI was opened everywhere to solve the mismatch; ~55% field-relevance for 2024 graduates and open commentary about AI as the new 'trap major' indicate the solution reproduced the problem one cycle later.
- Restructuring accelerated the very signal it was meant to correct. When the state and Fudan publicly devalue the humanities, applications collapse faster than any administrative decision could have cut them — the announcement did more than the policy.
- The exit metric corrupted the data. Employment-rate thresholds that determine programme survival generate falsified employment agreements, degrading the statistical base the whole system depends on.
- Faculty became the hidden adjustment variable. The policy discourse was about students and industries; the actual burden fell on mid-career academics, a constituency nobody planned for.
- Removing programmes did not remove students. Cutting 12,200 programme points while graduate numbers rose to 12.7 million means the queue was reorganised, not shortened — and the political attribution of unemployment shifted from macroeconomic policy to individual major choice, which is convenient and false.
- The new interdisciplinary category may outlast its contents. Creating a 13th degree category is a durable structural change; Embodied Intelligence and Brain-Computer Science may or may not be durable fields. China has built a permanent container for whatever is fashionable, which is either its smartest move or its most dangerous.
- Basic disciplines were cut before anyone noticed, requiring a corrective action line within two years.
- Elite institutions' prestige became detachable from the humanities, which will make it harder to restore them even if policy reverses.

PREDICTED FOR INDONESIA:
- ASYMMETRIC IMPORT PRODUCES PORTFOLIO INFLATION. Indonesia adopts the openings and not the closures, ending with more programmes than it started with, a higher share of them nominally strategic and substantively hollow. The single most likely unintended outcome.
- THE CHINA COMPARISON BECOMES A RHETORICAL WEAPON. '12,200 programmes cut in China' will be deployed in Indonesian debate to justify closures without the accompanying guard-rails — teach-out rights, faculty transition, basic-discipline protection, regional matching — that make the Chinese policy survivable. Selective citation of foreign policy is an Indonesian pattern.
- CLOSURE ENERGY IS DIVERTED TO INTEGRITY ENFORCEMENT. Because the ministry can revoke licences for fraud but cannot cull for irrelevance, the campaign becomes an anti-diploma-mill drive labelled as restructuring. Genuinely useful, but not the same thing, and it will be reported as if it were.
- TEACHER SHORTAGE IN THE 2030s. Intake cuts based on the 20,000-vacancy figure collide with the 679,000-shortage figure, producing a real shortage a decade out, precisely in the underserved regions.
- MATHEMATICS AND BASIC SCIENCE ATTRITION FORECLOSES THE AI AMBITION. Indonesia closes mathematics programmes while opening AI programmes, and discovers in ten years that it lacks the mathematicians to staff them.
- REGIONAL BRAIN DRAIN ACCELERATES. Ambitious students in eastern Indonesia, seeing local programmes closed or devalued, migrate to Java permanently — restructuring becomes a migration policy.
- PRIVATE-SECTOR CONSOLIDATION CREATES A NEW OLIGOPOLY. Large education groups acquire failing yayasan, producing a handful of national private chains with pricing power over the students least able to pay.
- THE DIAGNOSTIC REFORM SUCCEEDS AND THE REST IS NEVER NEEDED. The optimistic scenario, and genuinely plausible: publishing programme-level graduate outcomes shifts student demand so sharply that oversupplied programmes die of enrolment collapse — which is already the mechanism behind the 122 closures in 2026 — and Indonesia achieves the Chinese outcome without ever building the Chinese instrument. Markets do quietly what the Chinese state does loudly. This is the best available Indonesian path and it should be the explicit policy design.
kelompok_rentan:
(1) STUDENTS AND GRADUATES OF OVERSUPPLIED PROGRAMMES, ESPECIALLY TEACHER EDUCATION. ~490,000 a year against ~20,000 vacancies; ~450,000 annually at risk of educated unemployment. Disproportionately first-generation university students from lower-middle-income families outside Java, for whom the degree represented the family's largest single investment. They bear the full cost of a policy failure they did not create.

(2) LECTURERS AT SMALL PRIVATE INSTITUTIONS IN CUT FIELDS. Low pay, weak tenure, limited pension coverage, non-transferable specialisation, often the only white-collar employment in their district. China cushioned this inside state institutions; Indonesia has no cushion. Middle-aged humanities, education and generic-business lecturers outside Java are the single most exposed occupational group.

(3) STUDENTS AT INSTITUTIONS THAT FAIL OR LOSE THEIR LICENCE. 84 institutions flagged, 23-25 already revoked. Students face lost credits, unrecognised transcripts and interrupted study, with no adequate national teach-out or credit-portability framework.

(4) STUDENTS IN EASTERN INDONESIA AND REMOTE DISTRICTS. Cannot substitute a closed local programme with a distant one. For them closure is not redirection, it is exit from higher education. Compounded by the fact that these are the regions with the lowest participation rates to begin with.

(5) FIRST-GENERATION UNIVERSITY STUDENTS GENERALLY. They lack the family networks and information to read programme signals early, are most likely to choose a programme on affordability and proximity rather than outcomes, and are least able to absorb the cost of choosing wrong. Every information-poor decision environment stratifies against them.

(6) WOMEN, THROUGH A SPECIFIC AND UNDER-NOTICED CHANNEL. The programmes most exposed in both countries — teacher education, nursing and midwifery diplomas, humanities, languages, communications, design, generic business — are disproportionately female-enrolled, while the expanding fields (engineering, AI, robotics, semiconductors) remain male-dominated in Indonesia. Restructuring on the Chinese model therefore has a structurally gendered incidence: it cuts where women are and grows where they are not. Neither country's policy documents address this. Indonesia should, before rather than after.

(7) YAYASAN OWNERS AND STAFF AT SMALL PRIVATE INSTITUTIONS. Family-scale middle-class assets and the administrative staff attached to them.

(8) D3 DIPLOMA STUDENTS. Already being displaced by the D4 conversion; the 2026 closure list is dominated by D3 programmes. Students mid-way through a D3 in a converting institution face uncertain qualification value.

(9) STUDENTS ENTERING WEAK NEW PROGRAMMES — a group that does not yet know it is vulnerable. Anyone enrolling in an AI or robotics programme at an institution without qualified faculty, laboratory or industry partners is buying the Chinese failure mode at Indonesian prices, and will discover it four years later. Protecting this group is the cheapest intervention available today and requires only input gating on new permits.

(10) FUTURE SCHOOLCHILDREN IN UNDERSERVED REGIONS, if teacher-education intake is cut on the wrong number while a 679,000-teacher shortage persists. A diffuse group with no voice in the current debate and the most to lose from getting it wrong.
kasus_china:
CASE 1 — THE HEADLINE PROGRAMME: 12,200 REVOKED VS 10,200 CREATED. Across the 14th Five-Year Plan (2021-2025), Chinese universities revoked or suspended ~12,200 undergraduate programme points and created ~10,200, a net contraction of ~2,000 and cumulative churn above 30% of the national stock, with the annual adjustment ratio crossing 10% for the first time in 2025. Origin: the February 2023 five-ministry reform plan targeting ~20% adjustment by 2025. Escalation: the Central Education Work Leading Group's Action Plan (2025-2027) of 28 August 2025, with six action lines. Result: the target was exceeded by half again, and the campaign extended.

CASE 2 — INFORMATION MANAGEMENT AND INFORMATION SYSTEMS, THE ARCHETYPAL CASUALTY. 160 programme points revoked over 2020-2024, first place four consecutive years, plus 38 more in 2024 alone. A 1990s hybrid of business and IT that was cheap to open (no laboratory), taught almost identically at hundreds of institutions, and produced graduates who were neither managers nor engineers. Its death is the single cleanest illustration of what the campaign actually targets: not a discipline, but undifferentiated mass provision. The same logic killed Public Affairs Management (138), Information and Computing Science (123), Marketing (104), Product Design (93), Clothing and Apparel Design (70) and Educational Technology (51).

CASE 3 — FUDAN UNIVERSITY CAPS THE HUMANITIES AT 20%. President Jin Li announced that humanities and social science undergraduate intake would fall from a historical 30-40% to 20%, under the slogan 'refine the humanities, sharpen the sciences, strengthen engineering, renew medicine, enliven the interdisciplinary'. The 2025 class of 3,820 delivered it precisely: humanities and social sciences 776 (20.3%), sciences 737 (19.3%), engineering 778 (20.4%), medicine 765 (20.0%), interdisciplinary 764 (20.0%). China's most prestigious liberal-arts institution rebalancing to exactly one-fifth humanities was the permission signal for the entire system and the single most-debated act of the campaign.

CASE 4 — LOW-ALTITUDE TECHNOLOGY AND ENGINEERING: STATE CAPACITY TO CREATE A DISCIPLINE ON DEMAND. The low-altitude economy was designated a strategic emerging industry; MOE added 低空技术与工程 to the 2025 catalogue and approved six universities, led by Beihang, via an 'extraordinary' fast-track procedure bypassing the normal multi-year approval cycle. Elapsed time from industrial designation to first student intake: roughly 12-18 months. This — not the cutting — is the capability Indonesia most conspicuously lacks and could most usefully copy.

CASE 5 — THE 2026 INTERDISCIPLINARY CATEGORY. On 28 April 2026 MOE issued a catalogue with 883 majors, 92 major classes and, for the first time, a thirteenth top-level degree category: Interdisciplinary (交叉学科), containing 11 relocated majors plus four new ones — Embodied Intelligence, Brain-Computer Science and Technology, Future Robotics and Interdisciplinary Engineering — with nine universities including Harbin Institute of Technology and Beihang approved for embodied intelligence. The deepest structural change of the campaign: China stopped forcing new fields into old faculty boundaries and built a permanent home for whatever comes next.

CASE 6 — JIANGXI'S KILL SWITCH. Yellow card and enrolment-quota deduction for any programme below a 50% graduate destination rate; red card and enrolment suspension after two consecutive years below 50%; revocation under a 60%-for-2-3-years rule shared with Anhui. Five-year net: +312 programme points added, -335 stopped or revoked. Jiangxi and Fujian pioneered the mechanism from 2022. This is the operational core of the whole system — the point at which employment data becomes an administrative weapon — and it is the component least transferable to Indonesia.

CASE 7 — THE AI PROGRAMME BUBBLE, THE COUNTER-CASE. 621 institutions had registered AI undergraduate programmes by 2024, the most-added major of the decade. Chinese commentary now describes ordinary institutions opening AI to ride the trend without disciplinary strength, faculty 'learning while teaching', generic curricula, and institutions merely prefixing 'intelligent' to existing major names. Outcome: only ~55% of 2024 AI graduates in field-relevant work; about half judged the curriculum impractical or outdated; commentary warns AI may be the next 'trap major'. This case is more important for Indonesia than any of the others, because it is the mistake Indonesia is currently positioned to repeat.

CASE 8 — THE DISPLACED FACULTY. Following revocation of thousands of programme points, universities issued teacher redeployment surveys — one Hunan institution offering five tracks: adjacent-programme teaching, other technical posts, administrative posts, counsellor posts, and innovation-and-entrepreneurship college teaching. Humanities faculty were structurally disadvantaged by evaluation metrics weighted toward engineering outputs. The human cost of the campaign, borne by a group that appears in none of the policy documents.
padanan_indonesia:
(1) THE CLOSEST DIRECT EQUIVALENT — 122 PROGRAMMES CLOSED IN 2026. Indonesia's own restructuring number, discussed in parliament on 2 June 2026: 122 study programmes closed, all on institutional proposal. Most frequently: D3 Midwifery (16), D3 Informatics Management (8), D3 Accounting (7), D3 Computer Engineering (3), D3 Nursing (3), D3 Finance and Banking (3), S1 Retail Management (3), S1 Mathematics (2). Against ~30,000 programmes this is roughly 0.4% churn versus China's 10.1% — the same phenomenon at about one twenty-fifth the intensity, and driven by enrolment collapse rather than by policy. Note the structural difference: Indonesia's list is a D3-to-D4 conversion story, China's is an industrial-alignment story.

(2) THE TEACHER-EDUCATION OVERSUPPLY — INDONESIA'S 'INFORMATION MANAGEMENT AND INFORMATION SYSTEMS'. 6,844 education programmes, the largest field in the country ahead of engineering's 6,127, producing ~490,000 graduates a year against ~20,000 vacancies, with ~450,000 a year exposed to educated unemployment. Publicly raised by Secretary-General Badri Munir Sukoco at the National Population Symposium in April 2026, and described by critics as a Ponzi structure. This is Indonesia's single largest structural misallocation and its most exact analogue to what China cut — and simultaneously the least likely thing Indonesia will actually cut.

(3) UI'S S1 ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE — THE LAG MEASURED PRECISELY. Approved by UI's Academic Senate on 3 October 2025, first intake 2026/2027, at Fasilkom, aligned to the National AI Strategy 2020-2045, covering AI modelling, AI systems engineering and human-centric AI, taking Fasilkom to three undergraduate programmes. Set against China's first 35 approved AI programmes in March 2019, this dates the Indonesian creation-side lag at 6.5-7 years, measured flagship to flagship. UNIKOM's S1 Robotics Engineering and AI (2025/2026) and roughly 16 institutions with robotics offerings are the second wave.

(4) 'DIKTISAINTEK BERDAMPAK' AND THE 2026 PERFORMANCE CONTRACTS — THE INDONESIAN MECHANISM WHERE CHINA USED A QUOTA. Hundreds of institutional leaders signed 2026 performance contracts under an impact-oriented framework replacing graduate-count and publication-count metrics. Indonesia is attempting through negotiated performance agreements what China does through catalogue control — a genuinely different instrument aimed at a similar goal, and the natural vehicle if Indonesia ever wants to add outcome-based programme review without creating closure powers.

(5) THE MINISTERIAL FRAMING — 'TRANSFORMATION, NOT CLOSURE'. Minister Brian Yuliarto: closures are not ministry policy; programmes should transform (electrical engineering into AI, machine learning or robotics) with evaluation every 3-4 years; closure is a last resort where quality standards fail and mentoring cannot rescue. Combined with the ministry's explicit defence of basic sciences, social sciences, humanities and education as central to the national talent architecture, this is the precise inverse of the Chinese framing and the clearest evidence that Indonesia will import the trend selectively.

(6) THE INTEGRITY-DRIVEN EXIT MECHANISM. 84 private institutions flagged for possible licence revocation over unclear management, students and lecturers; 23-25 already revoked for diploma fraud and phantom enrolment; government commitment to relocate affected lecturers and students. This is Indonesia's actual functioning exit mechanism, and it targets fraud rather than strategic misalignment — a category difference from China's employment-rate kill switch that is easy to conflate and important not to.

(7) THE EMPLOYER PUSH. Deputy Minister Fauzan at the Employer Forum in Jakarta, 24 June 2026, calling for radical curriculum reform, replacement of theoretical lecture systems with adaptive curricula, professional class schemes and Centres of Excellence, explicitly framed as a response to graduate unemployment. The demand-side pressure that in China preceded the quota.

(8) THE PIPELINE MOVE. Kurikulum Merdeka 2026 adding coding and artificial intelligence as elective subjects nationally at school level, plus the national semiconductor talent programme with Kemenko Perekonomian and the Indonesia Semiconductor Hackathon 2026 — Indonesia building the feedstock before building the programmes, which is arguably better sequencing than China's.

(9) THE SYSTEM CONSTRAINT THAT DEFINES EVERYTHING. ~4,000+ institutions, roughly 30,000 programmes, ~8.2 million S1 students, only ~6% of institutions rated 'Unggul', gross participation ~32%, D4/S1+ unemployment 6.13% (Feb 2026) and rising. Indonesia's problem is a quality floor and an access ceiling simultaneously; China's was a capacity surplus. Same policy vocabulary, different disease.

On the Indonesian side: the 122 closures and the eight most-closed programmes (ministerial statement to parliament, 2 June 2026); the 6,844 education and 6,127 engineering programme counts (Directorate of Institutional Affairs, May 2026); the 490,000/20,000 teacher figures (Secretary-General, April 2026); UI's AI programme approval date and intake year (multiple outlets); February 2026 unemployment rates by education level (BPS).

MEDIUM CONFIDENCE: the total count of Indonesian study programmes and institutions (the most recent precise national totals I could confirm come from the 2020 statistics — 29,413 programmes, 4,593 institutions; current figures are inferred and marked uncertain); the number of Chinese universities offering AI (sources give 406, 499 and 621 for different definitions and dates — registration versus approval versus currently enrolling); the 55% field-relevant employment figure for 2024 Chinese AI graduates (widely circulated, original survey not verified); the estimated lag decomposition, which rests on defensible but arguable choices about which milestones to compare.

LOW CONFIDENCE: the humanities 7:1 supply-demand ratio and 2.3x unemployment multiple (Chinese commercial media, no official source); all timeline projections beyond 2030; the probability percentages, which are structured judgements rather than measurements; and the claim that no Indonesian equivalent exists for low-altitude/carbon-neutrality/embodied-intelligence degree programmes — this is a negative finding from search and could be wrong at an institution I did not sample.

METHOD NOTE: the China evidence is unusually strong for this research set because the policy is executed through published catalogues and annual ministerial releases, so figures are official rather than estimated. The main analytical risk is not data accuracy but interpretation — Chinese official framing presents restructuring as successful modernisation, and critical evidence (herd behaviour, faculty displacement, gaming, weak outcomes for new majors) had to be assembled from secondary Chinese sources that are individually less authoritative than the ministry but collectively consistent.

(1) THE INDONESIAN TEACHER PARADOX — the most consequential contradiction in this entire item. Kemdiktisaintek: ~490,000 teacher-education graduates a year against ~20,000 vacancies, i.e. massive oversupply. Kemendikdasmen: Indonesia is short roughly 679,000 teachers and is pushing PPG graduates toward 3T (frontier, outermost, disadvantaged) regions. Both are true and they describe different failures: an oversupply of credentials against a shortage of funded, filled positions in the places that need them. Resolution: the binding constraint is teacher formation (ASN/PPPK) and geographic distribution, not the existence of teacher education. POLICY IMPLICATION: cutting teacher-education intake on the strength of the 20,000 figure alone would be an error, and this contradiction should be resolved by a joint workforce plan before any restructuring decision is taken. Any Indonesian policy citing one figure without the other should be treated as motivated.

(2) CHINA'S 2024 ANNUAL FIGURES DIVERGE BY SOURCE. New programme points in 2024 are reported as both 1,839 (new points established) and 1,996 (added or adjusted); revocations as 1,428 with a separate 2,220 suspended from enrolment. The categories 'established', 'added or adjusted', 'revoked' and 'suspended' overlap in Chinese reporting and are not always distinguished in secondary coverage. The 12,200 headline is explicitly 'revoked OR suspended', which means the number of programmes actually deleted is lower than the number implies — a point systematically lost in international reporting, which frequently renders it as '12,000 degrees eliminated'.

(3) HOW MANY CHINESE UNIVERSITIES TEACH AI: 406, 499 and 621 all appear in credible sources for overlapping periods. These reflect different definitions (filed/registered versus approved versus currently enrolling), different dates, and inclusion or exclusion of vocational undergraduate institutions. Any single number should be treated as indicative.

(4) THE 20% TARGET IS NOT IN EVERY OFFICIAL DOCUMENT. The '~20% of discipline-major setting points by 2025' target originates in the February 2023 five-ministry reform plan and is widely restated in Chinese coverage, but the April 2025 MOE Q&A on the 2024 results does not restate it and instead emphasises qualitatively that revocations and suspensions substantially exceeded new establishments. This matters for interpretation: the target was real but the ministry prefers to present outcomes as structural optimisation rather than quota fulfilment, which is a familiar pattern when a quota is exceeded.

(5) CHINA'S POSITION ON THE HUMANITIES IS GENUINELY CONTRADICTORY, NOT JUST AMBIGUOUS. Fudan cut humanities intake to 20% and thousands of humanities-adjacent programme points were revoked — while the 2025-2027 Action Plan added a dedicated action line strengthening basic disciplines, the 2025 catalogue created 'new humanities' majors (AI Education, Digital Drama, Area and Country Studies), and Fudan's own slogan was 'refine the humanities'. International coverage resolves this contradiction in one direction ('China is killing the humanities') and Chinese official coverage in the other ('the humanities are being upgraded'). Both readings are partial. What is actually happening is the elimination of mass low-cost humanities provision alongside the creation of small elite and instrumentally-useful humanities programmes — a change in distribution, not merely in level.

(6) INDONESIA'S MINISTER CONTRADICTS INDONESIA'S OWN COVERAGE. Media report 'Kemendikti will close study programmes not relevant to industry'; the minister states that closure is not ministry policy, that the 122 closures were institution-proposed, that the focus is transformation, and that no education programmes were recommended for closure. Both are accurate at different moments — the ministry has floated relevance-based evaluation and then walked back the closure framing under criticism. Indonesian policy on this question is genuinely unsettled as of mid-2026, and this research should not be read as reporting a settled Indonesian direction.

(7) INDONESIAN SYSTEM TOTALS ARE STALE. The most recent precise national counts I could verify (29,413 programmes, 4,593 institutions) come from the 2020 Statistik Pendidikan Tinggi. The 2025 edition exists but its headline totals could not be extracted within this research (the PDF exceeded fetch limits and the PDDikti statistics portal returned 403). Current figures used here are inferred and marked uncertain; anyone using the closure-intensity comparison (0.4% versus 10.1%) should re-derive it from the 2025 statistics.

(8) NUMBERS DENOMINATED IN DIFFERENT UNITS ARE ROUTINELY COMPARED AS IF THEY WERE THE SAME. China counts 专业点 (programme points: one major at one institution). Indonesia counts prodi (also institution-level). These are comparable — but China's 883-major catalogue is a count of major TYPES, not points, and international coverage sometimes compares China's 12,200 points against a national catalogue of 883 types, producing nonsense. Care is required.

(9) THE 55% AI EMPLOYMENT FIGURE AND THE 7:1 HUMANITIES RATIO circulate widely in Chinese commercial and self-media without a traceable original survey. They are directionally consistent with everything else observed but should not be cited as hard data.
